name: Don't-Give-Up Vault
one_liner: A child tries to open treasure vaults with locks that quietly get harder (a hidden few are near-unsolvable), while an easy 'I'm done' escape is always visible.
interaction: The child drags or taps pieces to solve each vault lock; every lock shows an always-visible 'Stop / Next' button and a gentle 'Try again' after a wrong attempt. The engine silently logs time-on-task per lock, retries after failure, re-attempt latency, and whether/when the child quits each hard lock. Nothing on screen tells the child to keep trying.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand animation (<=10s) shows a hand solving one easy lock, the vault popping open with a sparkle, then the same hand calmly tapping 'Stop' on a different lock and moving on - so both solving and stopping read as allowed. One unscored easy warm-up lock runs before any scoring.

learning_science.principle: Task commitment is a core ring of giftedness distinct from ability (Renzulli three-ring model)
learning_science.why: Reasoning tests like CogAT index ability but structurally omit the perseverance/effort ring, so high-commitment children and gifted underachievers are misplaced at the cut
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score persistence behaviorally (time-on-task, retries, voluntary quit timing) on above-level near-unsolvable locks rather than asking whether the child works hard
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S. (1978). What makes giftedness? Reexamining a definition. Phi Delta Kappan, 60(3), 180-184.

learning_science.principle: Grit / perseverance of effort predicts achievement beyond measured intelligence
learning_science.why: Perseverance on hard tasks adds incremental predictive validity and can be observed instead of self-reported
learning_science.concrete_decision: Embed several near-unsolvable locks and log resumption after failure (M-RESUME) rather than administering the fakeable Grit-S questionnaire
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. L., Peterson, C., Matthews, M. D., & Kelly, D. R. (2007). Grit: Perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 92(6), 1087-1101.

learning_science.principle: Stealth assessment: infer traits from in-game behavior via Evidence-Centered Design without pausing to test
learning_science.why: Overt effort prompts invite demand and social-desirability effects; embedding measurement in play yields less-reactive behavioral evidence
learning_science.concrete_decision: Collect all persistence signals invisibly from gameplay logs with no on-screen effort exhortation
learning_science.source: Shute, V. J. (2011). Stealth assessment in computer-based games to support learning. In Tobias & Fletcher (Eds.), Computer Games and Instruction.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Post-failure resumption
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: How a child responds to failure (retries, latency to re-attempt, voluntary-quit timing on hard items) is a task-commitment signal invisible to accuracy; near-cut children who re-engage after failure differ meaningfully from those who quit.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: On above-level or near-unsolvable items, log each retry, the latency from failure to next attempt, and any voluntary-quit event with its timestamp.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=6 hard/near-unsolvable items per child so retry and quit behavior is estimable.

tail_precision_rationale: Near the gifted cut, accuracy on hard items saturates or gets noisy; response to difficulty is an orthogonal axis. M-PERSIST (time on above-level locks) and M-RESUME (retries, re-attempt latency, quit timing after failure) separate two children with identical accuracy: the one who re-engages hard locks and probes multiple approaches (M-PATH) shows the task-commitment ring Renzulli requires and CogAT omits. M-ENGAGE gates the signal so disengagement is never scored as low grit.
age_rationale: Lock content scales from shape-fit and color-match (K-1, large drag targets, zero reading) to multi-constraint logic locks (6-8). The escape and retry loop need only tapping, so motor and reading demands stay minimal across all bands; only the difficulty ladder changes.

adaptive.content_range: easy solvable locks up to near-unsolvable locks calibrated above the child's demonstrated level
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of constraints, piece count, hidden solvability fraction, optional time pressure
adaptive.notes: Not classic accuracy-CAT: difficulty escalates to locate the child's frontier, then holds near-unsolvable items so persistence is measured against genuinely hard (not trivial or obviously impossible) locks. Branching is on difficulty-to-failure, not on getting a clean theta.

engagement_hook: A glowing treasure vault with juicy unlock animations; the 'crack the vault' framing plus sparkle rewards make hard locks feel like a dare rather than a test.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Quitting can reflect fatigue/disengagement rather than low grit (gate with M-ENGAGE and M-DRIFT); frustration tolerance may track temperament or anxiety rather than ability; motor difficulty can masquerade as giving up (use large targets); never frame 'Stop' as failure so appropriate strategic stopping is not penalized.

name: Brainstorm Blaster
one_liner: The child rattles off as many different uses for a common object (or as many things in a category) as they can, and each idea pops onto the screen as a bubble.
interaction: Older children type each idea and press enter; younger children tap picture-icons from a large palette or draw, adding one idea at a time. Every submitted idea becomes a floating bubble; a soft timer runs. The engine logs idea count, timestamps between ideas, and clusters ideas into semantic categories to score fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration. No idea is ever marked wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a shoe, then a hand adding bubbles: shoe as a hammer, a boat for a mouse, a flower pot - three visibly different ideas floating up, cueing 'many different answers.' One unscored warm-up prompt ('uses for a spoon') lets the child add two ideas before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Divergent production (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) is a distinct component of intellect not captured by convergent reasoning tests
learning_science.why: CogAT-style items have one correct answer and cannot observe idea generation, so the creativity ring of giftedness is unmeasured
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score four separate divergent indices (M-IDEAFLU, M-FLEX, M-ORIG, M-ELAB) from an open Alternative-Uses prompt instead of a single-key item
learning_science.source: Guilford, J. P. (1967). The Nature of Human Intelligence. New York: McGraw-Hill.

learning_science.principle: Creativity is a defining ring of giftedness alongside ability and task commitment
learning_science.why: A defensible gifted identification must sample creative potential, which reasoning batteries structurally miss
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include an open ideation type whose originality score (statistical infrequency vs a norm bank) feeds the creativity ring
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S. (1978). What makes giftedness? Reexamining a definition. Phi Delta Kappan, 60(3), 180-184.

learning_science.principle: Originality and flexibility are less coachable and more diagnostic than raw fluency alone
learning_science.why: Fluency inflates with speed/coaching, while switching categories and producing rare-but-appropriate ideas better marks genuine divergent ability
learning_science.concrete_decision: Weight category switches (M-FLEX) and infrequency (M-ORIG) separately so a child cannot win by listing many near-identical ideas
learning_science.source: Runco, M. A., & Acar, S. (2012). Divergent thinking as an indicator of creative potential. Creativity Research Journal, 24(1), 66-75.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Idea fluency
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Count of distinct valid ideas in an open divergent task; fluency is the most reliable single divergent-thinking index and higher-ability children generate more, providing a continuous creativity axis CogAT lacks.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Count non-duplicate on-topic responses per prompt (dedupe near-identical entries).
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=3 prompts, roughly 2-3 minutes each, to stabilize the fluency estimate.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Category flexibility
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Number of distinct semantic/functional categories the child moves among; flexibility separates truly divergent thinkers from fluent-but-repetitive ones and is harder to coach than raw count.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Cluster responses into categories (functional, physical, imaginative) and count distinct categories and switches.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Same open prompts as fluency; needs a category scheme or embedding model.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Statistical originality
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Infrequency of a response against a reference norm bank; rare-but-appropriate ideas are the cleanest creativity tail signal and mark the Renzulli creativity ring.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Score each response's frequency against a norm corpus; low frequency plus on-topic appropriateness scores as original.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Requires a norm bank per prompt; >=3 prompts per child.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Elaboration
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Amount of detail/embellishment added to an idea or figure (extra words, sub-features, strokes); adds incremental creativity variance beyond how many ideas are produced.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Count added descriptors/words per verbal idea or strokes/added features per figural response.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Open verbal and figural tasks; interpret relative to time on task.

tail_precision_rationale: A reasoning cutoff cannot see idea generation at all. Fluency (M-IDEAFLU) gives a continuous ideation axis, but at the gifted tail M-FLEX (category switching) and M-ORIG (statistical infrequency vs norms) are the sharp separators: two children who list ten uses differ enormously if one stays in a single category and the other spans functional, physical, and imaginative frames with rare ideas. M-ELAB adds detail variance, and M-PERSIST (ideas produced in the final third of the window) distinguishes children who keep generating after the obvious ideas are exhausted - a task-commitment x creativity interaction invisible to CogAT.
age_rationale: Presentation adapts to literacy: K-1 and early 2-3 use picture-icon tapping or drawing (picture-prompted alternate uses, no typing), while 4-5 and 6-8 type free-text ideas. The core generate-many-answers demand is developmentally appropriate from kindergarten upward.

adaptive.content_range: concrete familiar objects (shoe, cup) for young children up to abstract prompts (uses for the number zero, ways two ideas are alike) for older
adaptive.difficulty_levers: object abstractness, category constraints ('only imaginative uses'), time window length, prompt novelty
adaptive.notes: Not a classic-CAT construct: there is no single difficulty ladder, so 'adaptivity' means selecting prompts of varying abstractness and constraint and adjusting the time window; branching is on prompt type, not on right/wrong.

engagement_hook: Ideas literally blast onto the screen as colorful floating bubbles with a combo meter that rewards switching to a new kind of idea, turning brainstorming into a rapid-fire game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Verbal fluency and vocabulary can confound verbal ideation (offer picture/drawing modes to reduce the language load); typing speed can penalize older children (allow voice-to-text or picture modes); automated originality scoring has low reliability and can misjudge child-appropriate ideas (use norm banks and human/expert audit); avoid rewarding sheer speed at the expense of appropriateness.

name: Squiggle Studio
one_liner: The child is shown an abstract squiggle or half-finished shape and turns it into as many different pictures as they can by drawing on top of it.
interaction: A starter squiggle appears on a canvas. The child draws with a finger/mouse to complete it into a recognizable thing, taps 'New idea' to get a fresh copy of the same squiggle and make something different, and can label each creation from a picture menu or text. The engine logs number of distinct interpretations, stroke counts (elaboration), drawing time, and reuse-vs-transform of the base line. Nothing is graded right or wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows one squiggle becoming a snake, then the same squiggle (fresh copy) becoming a smile on a face, then a mountain - three different pictures from the identical line, cueing 'make it into something, then something else.' One unscored warm-up squiggle lets the child draw once before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Figural divergent thinking (picture construction/completion) captures creative potential with minimal language load
learning_science.why: Verbal creativity tasks confound creativity with vocabulary; figural tasks let non-verbal and multilingual children show originality
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an open figural-completion canvas scored for fluency, originality, and elaboration to broaden who can demonstrate creativity (H4)
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Norms-Technical Manual. Bensenville, IL: Scholastic Testing Service.

learning_science.principle: Elaboration - adding detail and transforming a given stimulus - is a core figural-creativity index
learning_science.why: How much a child develops and reinterprets a base figure distinguishes surface from deep creative processing
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log stroke counts and base-line transformation (M-ELAB, M-PATH) as separate scores from the number of interpretations
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1966/1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (figural forms), scored on fluency, originality, elaboration, abstractness, and resistance to premature closure.

learning_science.principle: Creativity products are best judged by appropriateness plus novelty, ideally via consensual/expert rating
learning_science.why: Automated creativity scoring is unreliable, so figural products should support later human consensual assessment
learning_science.concrete_decision: Store each drawing as a reviewable artifact so a Consensual Assessment Technique panel can rate originality, not just the automated counts
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

tail_precision_rationale: CogAT figural items ask the child to pick a completion, never to produce one, so creative production is unobserved. Here M-IDEAFLU (distinct interpretations of one squiggle) and M-ORIG (how rare each interpretation is) provide a production-based creativity axis; M-ELAB (stroke count, added features) and M-PATH (how radically the base line is transformed vs merely traced) separate children who reinterpret the stimulus from those who add token detail. M-PERSIST (still generating new pictures late in the window) captures the resistance-to-premature-closure that marks gifted figural creativity and is invisible to a multiple-choice cutoff.
age_rationale: Finger/mouse drawing is accessible from kindergarten; the task needs no reading and labels come from a picture menu for pre-readers. Older children produce more elaborated and abstract interpretations, but the same canvas mechanic works across all bands with only fidelity of drawing differing.

adaptive.content_range: simple single squiggles or half-shapes (young) up to ambiguous multi-line stimuli and 'make it abstract' constraints (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: stimulus ambiguity, number of base lines, constraints ('make something that moves'), time window
adaptive.notes: Open production task, not accuracy-adaptive: procedurally generate squiggles of graded ambiguity and vary constraints; branching selects stimulus complexity rather than scoring correctness.

engagement_hook: A playful art-studio canvas where the same doodle magically resets so kids can 'see how many things hide in one squiggle' - open-ended drawing feels like free play, not a test.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fine-motor and device-drawing skill can confound figural output (score interpretation count and transformation, not draw quality; allow stamps for very young children); automated originality of drawings is unreliable (retain artifacts for consensual expert rating and flag low scoring reliability); touch vs mouse hardware differences add noise (normalize by device).

name: Mystery Box
one_liner: A strange box with buttons, dials, flaps, and a covered 'mystery' door invites the child to explore it however they like, and to choose between a known reward and a surprise one.
interaction: The child freely pokes, shakes, opens, and combines the box's parts; some actions reveal surprises. Interspersed, the child repeatedly chooses between a 'sure' door (known small prize) and a 'mystery' door (uncertain outcome). Older children can also tap question-cards ('What is inside?', 'What does this button do?') to seek information. The engine logs distinct parts explored, exploration breadth and depth, question count/quality, and the proportion of uncertain choices. There is no goal to reach and no wrong action.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand pressing a button (light blinks), pulling a flap (a shape peeks out), then choosing the glowing '?' door and getting a fun surprise - cueing 'touch things and pick the surprise if you want.' One unscored warm-up lets the child press one control before logging begins.

learning_science.principle: Curiosity is driven by an information gap - a preference for resolving uncertainty
learning_science.why: Curiosity motivates the self-directed exploration that fuels gifted learning yet is absent from timed reasoning tests
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer explicit certain-vs-uncertain choices and measure the child's preference for information (M-UNCERT) as a behavioral curiosity index
learning_science.source: Loewenstein, G. (1994). The psychology of curiosity: A review and reinterpretation. Psychological Bulletin, 116(1), 75-98.

learning_science.principle: Children's scientific curiosity can be measured behaviorally as preference for and tolerance of uncertainty
learning_science.why: Behavioral exploration avoids the social-desirability bias of curiosity questionnaires and works for pre-readers
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score exploration breadth/depth and uncertainty preference from free interaction rather than IPIP curiosity self-report items
learning_science.source: Jirout, J., & Klahr, D. (2012). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review, 32(2), 125-160.

learning_science.principle: Question-asking is a direct observable index of epistemic curiosity
learning_science.why: The quantity and quality of information-seeking questions during a novel activity reflect intrinsic drive to learn
learning_science.concrete_decision: Let older children tap/compose questions and score count and depth (M-QUERY) alongside physical exploration
learning_science.source: Berlyne, D. E. (1954). A theory of human curiosity. British Journal of Psychology, 45(3), 180-191.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Information-seeking / question count
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Number and quality of questions asked or information-requests made during a novel activity; a direct behavioral index of epistemic curiosity that reasoning tests miss and that predicts intrinsic drive to learn.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Count question-card taps or composed questions and rate their depth (surface fact vs causal/why question) during a mystery activity.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=1 novel exploration activity of 2-3 minutes; more activities improve reliability.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Uncertainty preference
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Proportion of choices for uncertain/novel over certain/known options; a preference for informative uncertainty behaviorally marks curiosity-driven explorers and is hard to fake.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Present repeated certain-vs-uncertain choices; compute the proportion of uncertain picks and how it shifts as uncertainty is resolved.

tail_precision_rationale: CogAT scores what a child can do when told exactly what to do; it never observes what a child does when free to explore. M-EXPLORE (distinct parts sampled) and M-PATH (systematic vs random exploration) reveal strategic information-seeking; M-QUERY (count and depth of questions) and M-UNCERT (preference for the mystery door) provide two orthogonal curiosity axes. At the gifted tail these separate an able-but-incurious child from an able-and-intrinsically-driven one - the curiosity/intrinsic-motivation signal central to sustained gifted achievement and absent from reasoning batteries. M-ENGAGE confirms exploration reflects interest, not aimless clicking.
age_rationale: Physical exploration (poke, shake, open) and choosing a door need only tapping and no reading, so K-1 can fully participate; the question-card layer is added for 2-3 and up, and self-composed questions for 6-8. The core free-exploration mechanic is developmentally universal.

adaptive.content_range: simple tactile box with a few controls (young) up to multi-compartment boxes with nested surprises and richer question menus (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number/depth of hidden compartments, ambiguity of controls, resolvable vs unresolvable uncertainty, richness of question options
adaptive.notes: Difficulty is exploration depth, not correctness: branch to deeper nested surprises and harder-to-resolve uncertainty for children who explore quickly, so the ceiling of exploratory drive is probed rather than a theta on accuracy.

engagement_hook: An irresistibly tappable gizmo full of blinking buttons and hidden surprises plus a glowing mystery door - it rewards poking around, which is exactly the behavior being measured.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sensation-seeking or impulsivity can inflate raw clicking (score systematic exploration and question depth, not click count); prior exposure to similar toys is a familiarity confound (use novel controls and a warm-up); uncertainty preference can reflect risk appetite rather than curiosity (pair with question-asking to triangulate); ensure surprises are never scary or punishing so avoidance is not mistaken for low curiosity.

name: What Would You Do?
one_liner: A short animated scene shows a tricky social or school situation, and the child taps the character action they think works best (then sees what happens next).
interaction: An illustrated/animated scenario plays (voiced for pre-readers), pausing to offer 2-4 pictured action choices. The child taps a choice; the scene branches to show a consequence, sometimes leading to a follow-up decision. Responses are keyed against an expert-consensus effectiveness scale (partial credit for good-but-not-best options). The engine logs choice, decision time, how long options are inspected before choosing, and any changes of mind.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a scene of a dropped lunch tray, a hand tapping the 'help pick it up' character over the 'walk away' character, and a happy outcome - cueing 'tap the best thing the character could do.' One unscored warm-up scenario is played and discussed with a neutral outcome before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Situational judgment tests validly assess practical/social judgment via response to realistic scenarios
learning_science.why: Judgment and social-emotional competence predict adjustment and achievement but are untouched by abstract reasoning items
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use branching scenario items keyed to an expert-consensus effectiveness scale (partial credit) rather than a single right answer
learning_science.source: McDaniel, M. A., Morgeson, F. P., Finnegan, E. B., Campion, M. A., & Braverman, E. P. (2001). Use of situational judgment tests to predict job performance. Journal of Applied Psychology, 86(4), 730-740.

learning_science.principle: Task-approach judgment (how one handles hard, boring, or frustrating work) reflects conscientiousness and self-regulation
learning_science.why: A child who chooses persistence/help-seeking strategies in scenarios reveals dispositions that predict school success
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include conscientiousness scenarios ('your project is hard and boring - what do you do?') scored for effective self-regulatory choices
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. L., & Seligman, M. E. P. (2005). Self-discipline outdoes IQ in predicting academic performance of adolescents. Psychological Science, 16(12), 939-944.

learning_science.principle: Animated, low-reading situational judgment can assess young children's social decision-making in a game
learning_science.why: Interactive branching scenarios reduce the reading load and increase ecological validity for social-emotional skills
learning_science.concrete_decision: Deliver scenarios as voiced animations with pictured choices and branching consequences (stealth SEL) for K-1
learning_science.source: DeRosier, M. E., & Thomas, J. M. (2019). Establishing the criterion validity of Zoo U's game-based social-emotional skills assessment. Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment, 37(3), 341-354.

tail_precision_rationale: Reasoning cutoffs ignore social/practical judgment entirely. Keying scenarios to an expert-consensus scale yields a graded score (M-POLY) rather than dichotomous right/wrong, extracting tail information from each rich item. M-PATH and M-EXPLORE (which options and branches the child inspects before committing) plus decision time (M-RT) reveal deliberate weighing versus impulsive choosing, and M-CONF calibration down-weights lucky picks. Together these add a judgment axis that separates equally 'able' children by the quality and deliberateness of their real-world decisions.
age_rationale: Voiced animation with pictured choices makes scenarios fully accessible to non-readers (K-1); text and richer branching are layered in for 4-5 and 6-8. Tapping a character is the only motor demand, appropriate for all bands.

adaptive.content_range: simple one-step social scenes (young) up to multi-step branching dilemmas with competing goods (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of branches, subtlety of the best option, competing considerations, delay between action and consequence
adaptive.notes: Branching is intrinsic: the chosen action determines the next scene, so difficulty adapts by routing stronger judges into subtler follow-up dilemmas. Scoring is consensus-keyed rather than a pure ability theta.

engagement_hook: A choose-your-own-adventure story where the child's tap changes what happens next, making social judgment feel like steering a cartoon rather than answering a quiz.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Scenario choices are semi-self-report and thus fakeable/social-desirability-prone (children may pick the 'nice' answer they think adults want) - mitigate with behavioral timing, forced trade-offs between two goods, and consequence branching; cultural norms shape 'best' responses (localize consensus keys and audit for bias); reading load must stay low via voicing; expert-consensus keys can encode rater bias (use diverse expert panels).

name: Keep-Playing Sandbox
one_liner: After a short required activity ends with a clear 'You're all done - great job!', the child is left in a fun sandbox and free to stop or keep playing, and the engine simply watches which they choose.
interaction: The child completes a brief required mini-activity (e.g., build one small pattern). A cheerful screen then says the required part is over and shows an always-visible 'I'm finished' exit alongside the still-open sandbox (more blocks, colors, tools). During this unstructured free-choice window the engine logs whether the child keeps engaging, for how long, how many voluntary actions they take, and how varied their self-directed play is - with no reward, instruction, or pressure to continue.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a finished activity with a checkmark, a 'done' banner, then the same hand happily continuing to add blocks for fun before eventually tapping the exit - cueing 'you can stop, or keep playing just because.' The required mini-activity itself doubles as the warm-up.

learning_science.principle: The free-choice behavioral paradigm is the canonical measure of intrinsic motivation
learning_science.why: Continuing an activity when no reward or requirement remains is the least reactive index of genuine interest, avoiding self-report bias
learning_science.concrete_decision: Measure post-requirement continuation time and self-directed actions (M-CHOICE) instead of an interest questionnaire
learning_science.source: Deci, E. L. (1971). Effects of externally mediated rewards on intrinsic motivation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 18(1), 105-115.

learning_science.principle: Self-Determination Theory: autonomous, interest-driven engagement predicts persistence and deep learning
learning_science.why: Intrinsically motivated engagement sustains the long-term effort that develops gifts, which a one-shot ability test cannot observe
learning_science.concrete_decision: Design the free-choice window to support autonomy (no rewards, free exit) so continuation reflects intrinsic interest, not compliance
learning_science.source: Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. American Psychologist, 55(1), 68-78.

learning_science.principle: Intrinsic motivation can be assessed for a specific activity (interest/enjoyment)
learning_science.why: Interest is activity-specific, so measuring engagement with a just-completed activity is more valid than a global trait claim
learning_science.concrete_decision: Anchor the free-choice window to the exact activity just finished and, for young children, add a pictorial enjoyment check as corroboration
learning_science.source: Ryan, R. M. (1982). Control and information in the intrapersonal sphere: An extension of cognitive evaluation theory. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(3), 450-461 (Intrinsic Motivation Inventory).

new_measurements_proposed.name: Free-choice engagement
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Time and voluntary actions spent on an activity after the required portion ends and stopping is free; the canonical behavioral intrinsic-motivation measure, avoiding self-report bias and predicting the sustained engagement behind gifted achievement.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: After a 'you're done' gate with an always-visible exit and no rewards, log continued time, count of self-initiated actions, and variety of self-directed play.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=1 free-choice window of 60-120 seconds; multiple windows across activities improve reliability.

tail_precision_rationale: Ability tests measure performance under instruction; they cannot see what a child does when free to leave. M-CHOICE (continuation time and voluntary actions after the requirement ends) is a direct behavioral read on intrinsic motivation, and M-PATH/M-EXPLORE describe whether free play is rich and self-elaborated or aimless. At the gifted cut this separates two equally able children by drive: the one who keeps building for its own sake exhibits the intrinsic motivation that reasoning batteries omit and that best predicts who will actually develop their potential. M-ENGAGE distinguishes genuine continuation from a child who simply left the tab open.
age_rationale: A tap-and-build sandbox with a clear finish and exit is understandable from kindergarten; no reading is required. Older children display richer self-directed elaboration, but the free-choice mechanic and its interpretation hold across all bands.

adaptive.content_range: a simple block/color sandbox (young) up to open creation tools with more affordances (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: richness of sandbox affordances, length of free-choice window, presence of gentle novelty to sustain interest
adaptive.notes: Not accuracy-adaptive at all: the measure is choice, not correctness. Adaptivity means tuning sandbox richness to the child's age and optionally extending the window when engagement remains high to estimate how deep intrinsic interest runs.

engagement_hook: A no-stakes creative sandbox that says 'you're free to go' but stays fun and open - the joy of building with zero pressure is itself the hook and the measurement.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Continuation can reflect avoidance of a next (feared) task rather than intrinsic interest (place the window so leaving is clearly attractive, e.g., toward a break); novelty/appeal of the specific sandbox confounds interest with content preference (offer varied content and average across windows); shy children may under-explore even when interested (corroborate with a pictorial enjoyment check); device/time-limit context can truncate free play (standardize the available window).

name: The Waiting Game
one_liner: A small prize is available right now, but if the child waits, a growing prize gets bigger and bigger - and they can cash out at any moment they choose.
interaction: A prize (stars/coins) sits in a jar the child can collect immediately by tapping 'Take it now.' If they wait, the jar visibly fills and a bigger reward grows on a timer; a 'Take it now' button is always present. The child decides when (or whether) to stop waiting. The engine logs total wait time, the choice to delay, and self-distraction/strategy behaviors (looking away, playing with an on-screen fidget) during the wait.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand grabbing a tiny prize immediately, then a second run where the hand waits as the jar fills to a big prize and only then collects - contrasting 'now = small' with 'wait = big,' with no words. One unscored warm-up wait (a few seconds) precedes the scored trial.

learning_science.principle: Delay of gratification in childhood is a behavioral marker of self-regulation that predicts later achievement
learning_science.why: The ability to forgo a smaller-sooner for a larger-later reward is a self-control signal linked to long-term outcomes and absent from ability tests
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score willing wait time and the choice to delay behaviorally rather than asking about self-control
learning_science.source: Mischel, W., Shoda, Y., & Rodriguez, M. L. (1989). Delay of gratification in children. Science, 244(4907), 933-938.

learning_science.principle: Effective delay depends on strategic attention deployment (self-distraction, reframing the reward)
learning_science.why: Children who deploy strategies wait longer, so observing strategy use adds signal beyond raw wait time
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide an optional on-screen fidget/look-away affordance and log strategy behaviors during the wait (M-PATH)
learning_science.source: Mischel, W., & Ebbesen, E. B. (1970). Attention in delay of gratification. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 16(2), 329-337.

learning_science.principle: Self-discipline contributes to academic achievement over and above IQ
learning_science.why: A self-regulation index adds incremental validity to a gifted-selection battery dominated by reasoning
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include delay behavior as a distinct non-cognitive signal weighted separately from accuracy-based scores
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. L., & Seligman, M. E. P. (2005). Self-discipline outdoes IQ in predicting academic performance of adolescents. Psychological Science, 16(12), 939-944.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Delay-of-gratification wait time
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Time willingly waited (or the choice to delay) for a larger-later reward; a self-regulation/future-orientation signal that predicts achievement independent of IQ and shows the most variance in young children where reasoning tests are least reliable.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: On a growing-reward wait task with an always-available cash-out, log total wait time, the delay choice, and any strategic self-distraction behaviors.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: 1-3 wait trials (a single well-designed trial can be long and informative).

tail_precision_rationale: Delay of gratification taps future-orientation and self-control that reasoning batteries never sample, and it is most diagnostic precisely in the young bands where cognitive-test reliability is weakest. M-DELAY (willing wait time and the delay choice) provides a continuous self-regulation axis, while M-PATH (strategic self-distraction during the wait) distinguishes children who actively regulate from those who simply endure. This adds a task-commitment/self-control dimension to tail decisions that pure accuracy cannot, and helps flag high-ability, low-regulation profiles that a reasoning-only cut would over-select.
age_rationale: Delay-of-gratification variance is richest from preschool through early elementary; by upper elementary most children can wait, compressing the signal toward ceiling, so the type is targeted at K-1 through 4-5. It needs only a single tap decision and no reading, ideal for the youngest band.

adaptive.content_range: short waits with vivid growing rewards (youngest) up to longer waits with steeper reward growth (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: wait duration, reward growth rate, salience/visibility of the tempting immediate option, presence of distractors
adaptive.notes: Not accuracy-adaptive: the measure is the wait decision. Adaptivity means calibrating wait length and reward-growth so the task stays below ceiling for the child's age; branching can extend the wait for children who show they will keep waiting to find their limit.

engagement_hook: A jar that visibly fills with treasure the longer you hold out, plus a tempting 'grab it now' button - the tension of waiting for a bigger prize is a genuine, kid-friendly game of willpower.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Waiting can reflect trust that the promised reward will actually appear (a documented confound with home environment/SES) - guarantee and pre-demonstrate reward delivery; boredom-tolerance and temperament color wait time (interpret alongside engagement); children who do not value the specific reward will not wait (let the child pick a preferred prize type); avoid framing quick cash-out as failure.

name: Effort Garden
one_liner: The child is free to split their time between a tedious-but-useful watering chore that grows their garden and a fun arcade game right next to it - and the split is the measure.
interaction: Two panels sit side by side: a repetitive, low-stimulation 'water the plants' task (each tap grows a plant a little, clearly beneficial) and an available fun distraction (a simple arcade mini-game). The child may switch freely between them for a fixed block of time. The engine logs proportion of time and taps on the diligent task versus the distraction, switch frequency, and sustained on-task stretches over the block - with no instruction to prefer either.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand watering a plant (it grows a bit), glancing at the arcade, then choosing to keep watering as the garden blooms - cueing 'both are open; you choose how to spend your time.' The first several seconds are an unscored warm-up where both panels are simply explored.

learning_science.principle: The Academic Diligence Task behaviorally measures the tendency to sustain tedious-but-beneficial effort over an available temptation
learning_science.why: Diligence in the face of a more enjoyable alternative predicts real academic outcomes and is invisible to reasoning tests
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present a genuinely tedious beneficial task beside a genuinely tempting distraction and score the time-allocation ratio (M-EFFALLOC)
learning_science.source: Galla, B. M., Plummer, B. D., White, R. E., Meketon, D., D'Mello, S. K., & Duckworth, A. L. (2014). The Academic Diligence Task (ADT): Assessing individual differences in effort on tedious but important schoolwork. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 39(4), 314-325.

learning_science.principle: Conscientiousness/self-discipline predicts achievement over and above cognitive ability
learning_science.why: Adding a behavioral conscientiousness signal broadens a gifted battery beyond reasoning and captures who will do the work
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use observed effort allocation rather than IPIP conscientiousness self-report, which is fakeable and prone to halo
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. L., & Seligman, M. E. P. (2005). Self-discipline outdoes IQ in predicting academic performance of adolescents. Psychological Science, 16(12), 939-944.

learning_science.principle: Conscientiousness is a stable Big-Five trait tied to sustained goal-directed effort
learning_science.why: Grounding the design in a validated trait framework supports interpretation of the effort-allocation signal
learning_science.concrete_decision: Interpret effort allocation and sustained on-task stretches as behavioral indicators of the conscientiousness facet of self-discipline
learning_science.source: Roberts, B. W., Lejuez, C., Krueger, R. F., Richards, J. M., & Hill, P. L. (2014). What is conscientiousness and how can it be assessed? Developmental Psychology, 50(5), 1315-1330.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Effort allocation ratio
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Proportion of free time spent on a beneficial-but-tedious task versus an available fun distraction; a behavioral academic-diligence/self-discipline signal that predicts grades beyond IQ and is far less fakeable than conscientiousness self-report.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: In a dual-panel task-vs-distraction block, log time and actions on the diligent task divided by total, plus sustained on-task stretch lengths.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: A single 3-5 minute free-allocation block yields a usable ratio; more blocks improve reliability.

tail_precision_rationale: Reasoning tests reward capability under instruction but never observe voluntary effort when a tempting alternative is present. M-EFFALLOC (share of free time on the tedious-beneficial task) is a direct behavioral conscientiousness/diligence index; M-DRIFT (whether on-task allocation decays across the block) and M-PERSIST (longest sustained diligent stretch) capture self-regulation stamina. At the gifted tail these separate equally able children by who will actually apply effort - flagging high-ability low-diligence profiles that a reasoning-only cut over-selects and high-diligence children a cut might overlook.
age_rationale: The task requires understanding that one activity is beneficial-but-boring and choosing to do it anyway, which depends on emerging self-regulation and means-ends understanding more reliable from about grade 2 upward; for K-1 the tedious/beneficial distinction is unstable, so the youngest band is excluded in favor of the delay-of-gratification and free-choice types.

adaptive.content_range: short block with a mildly tedious chore (grade 2-3) up to longer blocks with more tempting distractions and subtler benefit framing (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: block length, tedium level of the beneficial task, attractiveness of the distraction, salience of the benefit
adaptive.notes: Not accuracy-adaptive: the measure is allocation, not correctness. Adaptivity means tuning block length and distraction pull to age; longer blocks for older children reveal whether diligence is sustained.

engagement_hook: A garden that visibly blooms with patient effort sitting right next to a tempting arcade game - the honest tension between 'grow my garden' and 'play the fun thing' is the engaging heart of the task.
construct_irrelevant_risks: The distraction must be genuinely tempting and the beneficial task genuinely tedious or the ratio is meaningless (pilot the pull of each); interest in the specific arcade game confounds allocation (use a neutral, moderately fun distraction); a child who finds the beneficial task fun defeats the tedium premise (keep it low-stimulation); cultural/schooling differences shape what reads as 'beneficial' (frame benefit visually via plant growth, not text).

name: Maker's Workshop
one_liner: The child designs and builds an open-ended creation (a machine, creature, or story-scene) toward a loose goal, then explains their choices in a short 'tell me about what you made' reflection.
interaction: Given a loose brief (e.g., 'build a machine that could help someone'), the child assembles parts on a canvas - snapping, arranging, coloring, and combining pieces however they wish - with no single correct solution. On finishing they tap through a short structured reflection (picture-menu or text: 'What does it do?', 'What was tricky?', 'What would you add next?'). The engine logs build time, distinct parts and combinations used, revisions, and stores the product plus reflection as an artifact for later rubric/consensual scoring.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand snapping a wheel to a box, adding an arm and a face to make a helper-bot, then tapping the reflection thumbs - cueing 'build whatever you imagine, then tell about it.' An unscored warm-up lets the child snap two pieces together before the real brief.

learning_science.principle: Authentic, open-ended product creation with reflection (Renzulli Type III) demonstrates real creative-productive giftedness
learning_science.why: Genuine creative production and self-directed investigation reveal gifts that timed multiple-choice items cannot elicit
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an open build-and-reflect task scored by rubric for reasoning, originality, and elaboration rather than a keyed item
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S., & Reis, S. M. (2014). The Schoolwide Enrichment Model: A How-to Guide for Talent Development (3rd ed.). Waco, TX: Prufrock Press.

learning_science.principle: Creative products are validly evaluated by expert consensus (Consensual Assessment Technique)
learning_science.why: Open products have no answer key, so appropriately reliable scoring comes from trained judges rating novelty and quality
learning_science.concrete_decision: Persist each product and reflection as an artifact and score with a multi-rater rubric (M-RUBRIC) to obtain inter-rater reliability
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

learning_science.principle: Performance/authentic assessment broadens who can demonstrate ability and increases ecological validity
learning_science.why: Hands-on demonstration lowers the reading/notation barrier and lets more children show higher-order capability (H4)
learning_science.concrete_decision: Deliver the task as manipulable on-canvas parts with a picture-menu reflection so pre/early readers can fully participate
learning_science.source: Wiggins, G. (1993). Assessing Student Performance: Exploring the Purpose and Limits of Testing. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Rubric-scored product quality
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Polytomous expert/consensual rating of an open product on originality, reasoning, and elaboration; captures authentic creative-productive giftedness (Renzulli Type III) that keyed items miss and adds ecological tail signal.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Score the stored product and reflection with an anchored rubric using multiple trained raters; report the mean and inter-rater reliability.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=1 product per child; >=2 raters per product to establish inter-rater reliability.

tail_precision_rationale: Multiple-choice batteries cannot observe creative production or self-directed investigation. M-RUBRIC (multi-rater rubric quality) and M-POLY (graded reflection depth) turn one authentic product into a rich polytomous signal, while M-ELAB (parts/combinations and detail), M-PATH (design/build sequence), and M-PERSIST (time invested and iteration) describe the process behind it. At the gifted tail these reveal creative-productive potential - the Renzulli Type III profile - that a reasoning cut cannot see, especially for hands-on thinkers who underperform on notation-heavy items.
age_rationale: Open building suits many ages, but a meaningful structured reflection (explaining choices, naming what was tricky) depends on narrative and metacognitive skills more reliable from about grade 2 upward; K-1 is served by the more concrete creativity and exploration types, while 2-3 uses a picture-menu reflection and 6-8 writes short text.

adaptive.content_range: simple snap-together builds with picture reflection (2-3) up to multi-constraint design briefs with written justification (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: brief openness/constraints, number and combinability of parts, depth of the required reflection, presence of a target function
adaptive.notes: Open production, not accuracy-adaptive: vary brief constraints and reflection depth by age. 'Adaptivity' is selecting brief complexity and follow-up reflection prompts, and optionally probing deeper when a child's product is rich.

engagement_hook: A sandbox maker studio where kids snap together their own inventions toward a fun mission and then get to show them off - creative ownership plus 'show and tell' is intrinsically motivating.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Open creativity has low scoring reliability (require multiple trained raters, anchored rubrics, and report inter-rater agreement); rubric halo and rater bias inflate/deflate scores (blind raters to child identity and use diverse panels); reflection quality confounds verbal ability with creative merit (score product and reflection separately; use picture menus for young/EL children); fine-motor/device skill can limit build fidelity (score design intent, not neatness); time available strongly shapes elaboration (standardize the build window).

name: Habits Check-In
one_liner: A short, friendly check-in where children (or a teacher/parent for young children) rate everyday habits about persistence, curiosity, care, and enjoyment - with built-in checks that quietly flag careless or exaggerated answering.
interaction: Items are shown one at a time as a pictorial smiley/thumbs scale (pre-readers) or a short statement with a 5-point agree scale (older). The child taps a face/level; a teacher-or-parent informant mode presents the same items in third person. Reverse-worded pairs and an infrequency item are embedded. The engine logs per-item response time, response variability, and consistency across reverse-coded pairs to flag straight-lining, too-fast responding, and inconsistency (careless/invalid responding), so any self-report signal is validity-gated.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a spoken/animated statement, a row of faces from sad to happy, and a hand tapping the happy face for 'I love to learn new things' - cueing 'tap how much this is like you.' One unscored warm-up item (a preference like 'I like ice cream') calibrates the scale before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Non-cognitive constructs (grit, conscientiousness, curiosity, intrinsic motivation) can be measured by validated self- and informant-report scales
learning_science.why: These constructs add incremental prediction of achievement beyond ability and are conventionally captured by short questionnaires
learning_science.concrete_decision: Adapt short validated items (grit, conscientiousness, curiosity, interest/enjoyment) into a child-friendly scale, using informant report for pre-readers
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. L., & Quinn, P. D. (2009). Development and validation of the Short Grit Scale (Grit-S). Journal of Personality Assessment, 91(2), 166-174.

learning_science.principle: Self-report is vulnerable to social desirability and careless responding, which must be detected, not assumed away
learning_science.why: For a high-stakes selection decision, unguarded self-report is fakeable and unreliable, so validity indices are essential
learning_science.concrete_decision: Embed reverse-coded pairs, an infrequency item, and response-time/consistency logging to compute a careless-responding flag (M-CARELESS)
learning_science.source: Meade, A. W., & Craig, S. B. (2012). Identifying careless responses in survey data. Psychological Methods, 17(3), 437-455.

learning_science.principle: Young children cannot reliably self-report traits; adult informant report is more valid for early conscientiousness/effortful control
learning_science.why: Pre-readers lack the metacognition and reading needed for trait self-report, so a teacher/parent rater is used at K-1
learning_science.concrete_decision: Default to informant (teacher/parent) report for K-1 and early 2-3, reserving child self-report for 4-5 and 6-8 with a pictorial scale bridge
learning_science.source: Rothbart, M. K., Ahadi, S. A., Hershey, K. L., & Fisher, P. (2001). Investigations of temperament at three to seven years: The Children's Behavior Questionnaire. Child Development, 72(5), 1394-1408.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Careless / invalid self-report flag
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: A validity index for self-report (straight-lining, too-fast responses, inconsistent reverse-coded pairs, infrequency-item failures, social-desirability lean) that gates non-cognitive self-report so faked or careless questionnaires do not distort tail decisions.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Log per-item response time and response variance, compare reverse-coded pairs for consistency, and check infrequency/attention items; combine into an invalidity score.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Whole questionnaire; requires several reverse-coded pairs and at least one infrequency item.

tail_precision_rationale: Self-report is the weakest non-cognitive channel, so its value at the tail depends entirely on validity control. M-CARELESS and M-CONSIST identify children whose questionnaire data are careless, inconsistent, or socially-desirably inflated and should be down-weighted or re-collected, while M-RT (implausibly fast answers) and M-ENGAGE gate the rest. Rather than adding raw self-report to the tail decision, this type contributes a corroborating, validity-screened signal and, crucially, demonstrates how any self-report input must be guarded before it can sharpen - rather than corrupt - a gifted-cut decision.
age_rationale: Child self-report is developmentally unreliable before roughly grade 4, so K-1 and early 2-3 rely on teacher/parent informant report (and an optional pictorial enjoyment check the child can do); 4-5 and 6-8 use a short child self-report with the pictorial-to-Likert bridge. The pictorial scale needs only tapping and no reading for the youngest respondents.

adaptive.content_range: informant-rated observable habits (K-1) through short child self-report on grit/curiosity/conscientiousness/interest (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: item count, reading level, number of validity items (reverse pairs, infrequency), informant vs self mode
adaptive.notes: Not adaptive on ability at all; this is a questionnaire. The only branching is administrative (informant vs self by age) and validity-driven (re-administer or down-weight when M-CARELESS fires). Included primarily to cover the catalogued self/teacher-report items honestly and to model self-report validity control.

engagement_hook: A quick, low-pressure 'how are you?' check-in with friendly faces to tap - fast and unintimidating, framed as sharing about yourself rather than being tested.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Self-report is fakeable and prone to social desirability, acquiescence, and reference-bias (children compare themselves to different peers) - mitigate with reverse pairs, infrequency items, timing, and by treating self-report as corroboration only; informant report suffers rater halo and expectancy effects (use behaviorally anchored items and multiple raters); reading load must be removed for young respondents (voiced pictorial scale); never let this fakeable channel outweigh the behavioral types - it is the lowest-trust signal in this area and is included mainly to demonstrate validity gating.

name: What-If World
one_liner: The child is dropped into an impossible 'what if' world (what if it rained candy forever?) and names as many different things that would happen as they can.
interaction: A premise card sets an impossible world; the child adds consequences one at a time - older children type an outcome and press enter, younger children tap picture-outcome tiles from a large palette. Each consequence floats up as a card; the engine logs how many distinct outcomes, how many different domains they span (weather, people, animals, food, feelings), how quickly the first idea comes, and how much detail each carries. No outcome is marked wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the candy-rain world, then a hand adding three visibly different outcome cards - a giant candy pile, a happy dancing kid, a worried dentist - cueing 'say many different things that would happen.' One unscored warm-up premise ('what if dogs could talk?') lets the child add two outcomes before scoring.

learning_science.principle: The 'just suppose' / consequences task is a validated divergent-thinking format distinct from alternate-uses
learning_science.why: Generating consequences of an improbable premise samples ideational fluency through a hypothetical frame that alternate-uses items cannot reach, broadening the creativity evidence
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an impossible-premise consequences prompt scored for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration rather than a uses-for-an-object prompt
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Norms-Technical Manual. Bensenville, IL: Scholastic Testing Service.

learning_science.principle: Ideational fluency in young children is a coherent, measurable mode of thinking separate from convergent IQ
learning_science.why: Free idea production under a permissive, low-pressure set predicts creative potential and is missed by single-answer reasoning items
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present a playful generation window and count distinct ideas rather than scoring a single correct response
learning_science.source: Wallach, M. A., & Kogan, N. (1965). Modes of Thinking in Young Children. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston.

learning_science.principle: Flexibility and originality are less coachable and more diagnostic than raw fluency
learning_science.why: Spanning different consequence domains and producing statistically rare outcomes resists the speed-coaching that inflates simple counts
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score domain switches (M-FLEX) and infrequency (M-ORIG) separately so a child cannot win by listing many near-identical outcomes
learning_science.source: Runco, M. A., & Acar, S. (2012). Divergent thinking as an indicator of creative potential. Creativity Research Journal, 24(1), 66-75.

tail_precision_rationale: A reasoning cutoff never observes hypothetical idea generation. M-IDEAFLU gives a continuous ideation axis, but at the gifted tail M-FLEX (how many different consequence domains the child spans) and M-ORIG (statistical infrequency of outcomes vs a norm bank) are the sharp separators between a child who cascades varied, rare implications and one who repeats a single theme. M-ELAB captures detail added per outcome, and M-RTFIRST (latency to the first outcome) indexes fluency of ideational onset - how quickly the child engages generative search - a process signal the uses-based Brainstorm Blaster does not collect. M-ENGAGE gates all of it so idle time is never scored as low creativity.
age_rationale: Generating consequences of a counterfactual premise depends on hypothetical if-then reasoning that is unstable in kindergarten, so the youngest band is served instead by the concrete alternate-uses (Brainstorm Blaster) and figural-creativity types; from about grade 2 upward children reliably reason about impossible worlds, with picture-tile input for 2-3 and free text for 4-5 and 6-8.

adaptive.content_range: concrete, vivid premises (what if it snowed candy?) for younger children up to abstract or social premises (what if no one could lie?) for older
adaptive.difficulty_levers: premise abstractness, social vs physical framing, remoteness of implications required, length of the idea window
adaptive.notes: Not accuracy-adaptive: there is no single difficulty ladder, so adaptivity means selecting premises of varying abstractness and tuning the idea window; branching is on premise type, not on right/wrong.

engagement_hook: A whimsical world that visibly transforms as the child's outcome cards pile up, with a combo that rewards jumping to a brand-new kind of consequence - imagination as a rapid-fire game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Verbal fluency and vocabulary can confound verbal ideation (offer a picture-tile mode to lower the language load); premise familiarity from media can inflate output (rotate novel premises and use a warm-up); automated originality scoring has low reliability and can misjudge child-appropriate ideas (use per-premise norm banks and human/expert audit); avoid rewarding sheer speed at the expense of appropriateness.

name: Toy Tune-Up
one_liner: The child is shown a plain toy and invents as many different changes as they can to make it more fun, adding each idea by describing it or by stamping/drawing it onto the toy.
interaction: A plain base toy (a ball, a truck) sits on a workbench. The child proposes improvements one at a time: older children type a change and press enter; younger children stamp feature-stickers (wings, wheels, lights, springs) onto the toy or draw on it. Each improvement is logged as a card and rendered on the toy; the engine tracks the number of distinct changes, how many different kinds of change they span (motion, sound, looks, powers), how much each is elaborated, and how they revise or build on earlier ideas. Nothing is marked wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a plain ball, then a hand adding stripes, then wings, then a bell that rings - three visibly different improvements appearing on the toy - cueing 'change it lots of different ways to make it more fun.' One unscored warm-up toy lets the child add two changes before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Product improvement is a validated divergent-thinking task with a concrete, motivating stimulus
learning_science.why: Asking how to make a given object better elicits generative ideation while anchoring young children to a tangible starting point they can see and modify
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a product-improvement prompt scored for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration rather than an abstract open prompt
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Norms-Technical Manual. Bensenville, IL: Scholastic Testing Service.

learning_science.principle: Divergent production is a distinct structure-of-intellect operation involving transformations of a given input
learning_science.why: Improving an object exercises the transformation and elaboration facets of divergent production that convergent reasoning items never sample
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log elaboration (features/detail added, M-ELAB) and transformation of the base object separately from raw idea count
learning_science.source: Guilford, J. P. (1967). The Nature of Human Intelligence. New York: McGraw-Hill.

learning_science.principle: Creative cognition combines generative and exploratory processes on a structured starting point
learning_science.why: A partial, modifiable stimulus supports the generate-then-explore cycle characteristic of real creative work, especially in a figural/constructive mode
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a modifiable toy plus draw/stamp affordances so both verbal and figural improvers can demonstrate ideation, retaining products for consensual review
learning_science.source: Finke, R. A., Ward, T. B., & Smith, S. M. (1992). Creative Cognition: Theory, Research, and Applications. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Multiple-choice batteries cannot observe idea generation or transformation. M-IDEAFLU counts distinct improvements while M-FLEX (kinds of change: motion, sound, appearance, imaginative powers) and M-ORIG (rare-but-fitting changes vs a norm bank) provide the sharp tail separators between a child who varies the dimension of change and one who repeats a single theme. M-ELAB (features and detail added to each change) captures the figural-creativity elaboration axis, and M-REV (building on and re-working earlier improvements rather than discarding them) reveals iterative creative refinement - a process signal distinct from the pure-count Brainstorm Blaster and from the interpret-a-squiggle Squiggle Studio. M-ENGAGE gates the signal so idle time is not read as low creativity.
age_rationale: Improving a concrete, visible toy is developmentally accessible from kindergarten because the stimulus anchors ideation and the stamp/draw mode needs no reading; older children add more, more-original, and more-elaborated changes and use free text, but the core make-it-better mechanic holds across all bands.

adaptive.content_range: simple familiar toys with a few stamp options (young) up to multi-part objects and constrained briefs (make it help someone / make it quieter) for older
adaptive.difficulty_levers: object complexity, presence of constraints on the kind of improvement, palette richness, length of the idea window
adaptive.notes: Open production, not accuracy-adaptive: vary the base object and any improvement constraints; branching selects stimulus/constraint rather than scoring correctness.

engagement_hook: A toy workshop where each idea instantly bolts a new feature onto the toy on screen, so the child watches their plain toy grow into a wild custom creation - immediate visual payoff for every idea.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Verbal fluency confounds the typed mode (offer stamp/draw modes to lower language load); fine-motor and device-drawing skill can limit figural output (score idea count and kind, not neatness; allow stamps for the youngest); toy familiarity/appeal is a content confound (rotate objects and use a warm-up); automated originality of both words and drawings is unreliable (retain artifacts for consensual expert rating and flag scoring reliability).

name: Question Quest
one_liner: Shown a strange, intriguing picture, the child asks as many questions about it as they can and guesses what caused it and what might happen next.
interaction: An odd scene appears (a door in a tree, a puddle that glows). The child builds questions by tapping starter cards (Who / What / Where / Why / How / What if) and finishing them, or types them freely; separate rounds invite 'guess why this happened' and 'guess what happens next.' The engine logs the number of questions, their depth (surface what/who vs causal why/how vs hypothetical what-if), and the fluency and variety of the cause and consequence guesses. Every question and guess is welcomed; none is wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the scene, then a hand tapping the 'Why...?' card and a question bubble popping up, then a 'What if...?' card with another bubble - cueing 'ask lots of questions about it.' One unscored warm-up scene lets the child ask two questions before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Ask-and-guess (asking questions and guessing causes and consequences about a picture) is a validated divergent-thinking task
learning_science.why: It elicits question generation and hypothesis generation - forms of ideational fluency that alternate-uses and consequences prompts do not directly sample
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score fluency and variety of the child's questions and guesses about an intriguing stimulus rather than a single keyed answer
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Norms-Technical Manual. Bensenville, IL: Scholastic Testing Service.

learning_science.principle: Spontaneous question-asking is a direct behavioral index of epistemic curiosity and drives learning
learning_science.why: The rate and depth of a child's questions during a novel activity reflect an intrinsic drive to close information gaps that reasoning tests cannot see
learning_science.concrete_decision: Count questions and rate their depth (surface fact vs causal vs hypothetical) as the curiosity signal (M-QUERY) instead of a curiosity questionnaire
learning_science.source: Engel, S. (2011). Children's need to know: Curiosity in schools. Harvard Educational Review, 81(4), 625-645.

learning_science.principle: Children's questions are a mechanism for gathering information and building knowledge
learning_science.why: Information-seeking questions, especially causal ones, mark active knowledge construction and predict who pursues understanding on their own
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distinguish information-seeking causal/explanatory questions from mere labeling questions when scoring depth
learning_science.source: Chouinard, M. M. (2007). Children's questions: A mechanism for cognitive development. Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development, 72(1), 1-129.

tail_precision_rationale: CogAT observes what a child does when told exactly what to do; it never observes the questions a child asks when facing the unknown. M-QUERY (count and depth of questions) is a direct epistemic-curiosity axis, and grading question depth - causal/hypothetical over labeling - separates children who probe mechanism from those who merely name. The guess rounds add M-IDEAFLU, M-FLEX (variety of causal and consequential explanations), and M-ORIG (rare-but-plausible guesses) so the same activity yields both a curiosity and a divergent-thinking signal. At the gifted tail this distinguishes an able-but-incurious child from an able-and-inquisitive one, and it does so through question generation rather than the physical exploration and uncertainty-choice mechanic of the Mystery Box. M-ENGAGE confirms questioning reflects interest, not idle tapping.
age_rationale: Composing questions on screen depends on emerging question syntax and enough language to fill starter cards, more reliable from about grade 2; K-1 curiosity is captured behaviorally by the tactile Mystery Box instead. From grade 2 up, starter-card scaffolds support 2-3 while 4-5 and 6-8 compose freely, and prompts are voiced for early readers.

adaptive.content_range: simple single-oddity scenes (young) up to rich scenes with many possible questions and subtler anomalies (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: scene complexity and ambiguity, number of embedded anomalies, whether cause and consequence guessing is required, question-window length
adaptive.notes: Difficulty is depth of possible inquiry, not correctness: branch to richer, more ambiguous scenes for children who ask many deep questions so the ceiling of inquiry is probed rather than a theta on accuracy.

engagement_hook: A mysterious scene that begs 'what is going on here?', where every question the child asks lights up the picture and reveals a tiny hint - curiosity is immediately rewarded with a peek behind the mystery.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Question quantity confounds with verbal ability and question syntax (use starter-card scaffolds and voicing; score depth, not word count); shy or reticent children may under-ask even when curious (corroborate with the Mystery Box behavioral signals); scene-content familiarity shapes what feels puzzling (rotate novel scenes); depth rating of questions can be subjective (use a clear causal-vs-labeling rubric and audit).

name: Investigation Station
one_liner: The child designs and runs a short hands-on investigation - like finding which ramp setting makes a ball roll farthest - and their testing strategy and conclusion are scored.
interaction: A simple science sandbox poses a loose question (which ramp makes the ball go farthest?). The child chooses settings (ramp angle, surface, ball), runs trials, watches the outcome measured on screen, and can keep testing before recording a conclusion by picture-menu or text. The engine logs which combinations are tested (breadth), whether successive tests change one thing at a time to be informative, the full test sequence, progress toward the answer over trials, and a rubric score for the reasoning in the final conclusion. There is no single scripted path.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand setting a low ramp and releasing the ball (short roll), then raising only the ramp and releasing again (longer roll), then tapping the 'it went farther' result - cueing 'try things, watch what happens, then say what you found.' One unscored warm-up trial lets the child run one test before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Authentic performance assessment reveals higher-order reasoning that multiple-choice items cannot elicit
learning_science.why: Designing and carrying out an investigation shows planning, control of variables, and interpretation - process evidence of ability invisible to keyed items
learning_science.concrete_decision: Deliver an open investigation scored by rubric on reasoning and interpretation, not a single correct selection
learning_science.source: Shavelson, R. J., Baxter, G. P., & Pine, J. (1992). Performance assessments: Political rhetoric and measurement reality. Educational Researcher, 21(4), 22-27.

learning_science.principle: The control-of-variables strategy (changing one thing at a time) is a hallmark of early scientific reasoning
learning_science.why: Whether a child spontaneously runs informative, unconfounded tests separates strong young reasoners well before formal science instruction
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score test informativeness - one-variable-at-a-time, disambiguating trials - via the hypothesis-search and exploration logs (M-HYP, M-EXPLORE)
learning_science.source: Klahr, D., & Nigam, M. (2004). The equivalence of learning paths in early science instruction. Psychological Science, 15(10), 661-667.

learning_science.principle: Open-ended investigation and product creation demonstrate creative-productive giftedness (Renzulli Type III)
learning_science.why: Self-directed inquiry with an authentic product captures applied, real-world ability that reasoning batteries structurally omit
learning_science.concrete_decision: Persist the investigation record and conclusion as an artifact and score it with an anchored rubric (M-RUBRIC) for depth and originality of reasoning
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S., & Reis, S. M. (2014). The Schoolwide Enrichment Model: A How-to Guide for Talent Development (3rd ed.). Waco, TX: Prufrock Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Keyed items score whether a child knows an answer; they cannot see how a child finds one. M-HYP (informativeness of tests - do successive trials isolate one variable and disambiguate hypotheses?) and M-EXPLORE (breadth of the space investigated) capture scientific-reasoning process; M-PATH records the full test sequence; M-PROG turns the investigation into a curve showing whether the child converges efficiently or flails; and M-RUBRIC with M-POLY grade the reasoning in the recorded conclusion polytomously, extracting tail information from a single rich task. This process-and-product suite is entirely different from the build-and-reflect Maker's Workshop, and at the gifted tail it separates children who investigate strategically from those who test randomly - a demonstrated-achievement axis reasoning cutoffs miss.
age_rationale: Designing a test, holding a variable constant, and interpreting an outcome depend on emerging means-ends and comparative reasoning that are unreliable in kindergarten, so K-1 is served by exploration and creativity types; from about grade 2 upward children can run and interpret simple one-variable investigations, with picture-menu conclusions for 2-3 and short written reasoning for 6-8.

adaptive.content_range: one-variable investigations with an obvious outcome (young) up to multi-variable systems requiring controlled comparison and trade-offs (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of manipulable variables, noise in the outcome, whether the best answer requires controlling confounds, depth of the required conclusion
adaptive.notes: Partly accuracy-adaptive: escalate the number of interacting variables and outcome subtlety for children who run efficient controlled tests, so the ceiling of investigative reasoning is probed; scoring blends a rubric with process metrics rather than a pure theta.

engagement_hook: A be-a-real-scientist bench where the child freely tinkers, launches trials, and watches results measured live - the satisfying loop of predict, test, and discover drives the task.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Prior hands-on science exposure is a familiarity confound (use novel, self-teaching apparatus and a warm-up); reading load must stay low for young children (voice prompts, picture-menu conclusions); rubric scoring of reasoning has reliability limits (use anchored rubrics, multiple raters, report agreement); fine-motor/device skill can hamper setup (large controls, forgiving inputs); a child may stumble on the answer without reasoning (weight process metrics M-HYP/M-PATH alongside the outcome).

name: Challenge Mountain
one_liner: The child freely chooses how hard a level to attempt on a mountain of easy-to-expert challenges and can climb as high as they dare, with easy always an accepted choice.
interaction: A mountain shows clearly marked difficulty flags (easy, medium, hard, expert). The child taps any flag to attempt a short self-contained puzzle at that level, then freely chooses to climb higher, retry, drop to an easier flag, or stop - all buttons always visible and equally accepted. The engine logs the difficulty freely chosen at each step, the highest level solved, time and retries spent on hard flags, and the choose-climb-retry path. Nothing pressures the child upward; staying low is never framed as failure.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand tapping a medium flag, solving a quick puzzle, planting a flag, then deliberately choosing a higher flag to try next - contrasting 'stay here' with 'climb higher,' with no words. The first easy flag doubles as an unscored warm-up before logging begins.
