learning_science.principle: A behavioral preference for challenge is a core marker of intrinsic, mastery-oriented motivation
learning_science.why: Choosing harder tasks when easier ones are freely available reveals intrinsic mastery motivation that self-report scales measure only indirectly
learning_science.concrete_decision: Let the child freely select difficulty and score the voluntary challenge level chosen (M-CHOICE) rather than asking whether they like hard work
learning_science.source: Harter, S. (1981). A new self-report scale of intrinsic versus extrinsic orientation in the classroom. Developmental Psychology, 17(3), 300-312.

learning_science.principle: Mastery (learning) goals drive children to seek challenge and persist, whereas performance goals drive avoidance
learning_science.why: Challenge-seeking and persistence after difficulty behaviorally distinguish the achievement-goal orientation that predicts long-run development of ability
learning_science.concrete_decision: Interpret voluntary difficulty escalation and post-failure retries as behavioral indicators of a mastery orientation, gating on engagement
learning_science.source: Dweck, C. S. (1986). Motivational processes affecting learning. American Psychologist, 41(10), 1040-1048.

learning_science.principle: Task commitment is a distinct ring of giftedness alongside ability and creativity (Renzulli)
learning_science.why: Voluntary challenge-seeking and sustained effort on hard, self-chosen tasks are exactly the task-commitment behaviors reasoning tests omit
learning_science.concrete_decision: Combine the challenge chosen with persistence and resumption on hard flags (M-PERSIST, M-RESUME) to index the task-commitment ring behaviorally
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S. (1978). What makes giftedness? Reexamining a definition. Phi Delta Kappan, 60(3), 180-184.

tail_precision_rationale: Reasoning cutoffs measure capability under an assigned difficulty; they never observe the difficulty a child chooses when free. M-CHOICE (the voluntary difficulty selected when easy is equally allowed) and M-DIFFREACH (the highest level actually solved under self-selection) provide a mastery-motivation axis, while M-PERSIST and M-RESUME (time and retries invested on hard flags after failure) distinguish children who push their edge from those who retreat to comfort. M-PATH captures the climb-retry-drop pattern. This voluntary-challenge shell is distinct from the Don't-Give-Up Vault, which assigns near-unsolvable items and measures endurance; here the signal is what the child elects to attempt. At the gifted tail this separates equally able children by drive - flagging high-ability children who avoid challenge and revealing high-commitment climbers a reasoning-only cut would miss. M-ENGAGE ensures climbing reflects motivation, not random tapping.
age_rationale: Choosing a flag and deciding whether to climb needs only tapping and a visible easy-to-hard ladder, so kindergarteners can participate fully; puzzle content at each flag scales by band while the choose-your-challenge mechanic and its interpretation hold across all ages.

adaptive.content_range: a short low ladder with vivid, simple puzzles (young) up to a tall ladder with genuinely hard expert puzzles well above grade level (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: ladder height and spacing, puzzle content per flag, how far above grade level the expert flags reach, availability of an always-open easy option
adaptive.notes: Self-adaptive by design: the child sets their own difficulty, so the type naturally locates a motivational frontier; M-DIFFREACH also yields an ability ceiling as a by-product, but the primary signal is the freely chosen challenge, not a fitted theta.

engagement_hook: A climbable mountain where conquering a flag plants your banner and unlocks the daring option to go higher - the pull to see how far up you can get turns effort into an adventure.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Challenge choice can reflect risk appetite, confidence, or prior success rather than mastery motivation (triangulate with persistence and resumption, not choice alone); anxious or perfectionistic able children may avoid hard flags despite high ability (never frame easy as failure; interpret with other non-cognitive types); content familiarity at each flag confounds the difficulty felt (calibrate and rotate puzzles); the ladder ceiling must exceed the child's ability or M-DIFFREACH truncates.

name: Idea Round-Up
one_liner: The child rattles off as many different things as they can that fit a simple property (all the round things, all the things that make noise), tapping matching pictures and adding their own.
interaction: A wordless category cue is shown (a shape morphs among a ball, a sun, and a wheel to signal 'round things'). A lively field of picture tiles drifts on screen; the child taps every tile that fits the category to send it into a basket, and taps a '+' to add an idea of their own by drawing, stamping, or (older) typing. Each accepted idea joins the basket and a soft timer runs. The engine logs how many distinct fitting ideas are produced, how many different sub-kinds they span, how rare each idea is, and how much of the field the child sampled. No tap is ever marked wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the morphing 'round' cue, then a hand tapping a ball, an orange, and a coin - three visibly different round things flying into the basket while a counter ticks up - cueing 'find and add many different things like this.' One unscored warm-up category ('things that are round') lets the child add two ideas before scoring begins.

learning_science.principle: Ideational fluency (generating many instances of a class) is a coherent mode of thinking in young children, separable from convergent IQ
learning_science.why: Free instance generation under a permissive set surfaces creative potential in pre- and early readers that single-answer reasoning items cannot observe
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the number of distinct on-category instances (M-IDEAFLU) from an open Instances prompt with picture-tap input for non-readers rather than a keyed item
learning_science.source: Wallach, M. A., & Kogan, N. (1965). Modes of Thinking in Young Children. New York: Holt, Rinehart & Winston.

learning_science.principle: Category flexibility and statistical originality are less coachable and more diagnostic than raw fluency
learning_science.why: Spanning different sub-categories and producing rare-but-fitting instances resists the speed-coaching that inflates simple counts
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score distinct sub-categories and switches (M-FLEX) and infrequency (M-ORIG) separately so listing many near-identical instances cannot win
learning_science.source: Runco, M. A., & Acar, S. (2012). Divergent thinking as an indicator of creative potential. Creativity Research Journal, 24(1), 66-75.

learning_science.principle: Creativity is a defining ring of giftedness alongside ability and task commitment
learning_science.why: A defensible gifted identification must sample creative potential, which reasoning batteries structurally miss
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include an open ideational-fluency type whose flexibility and originality feed the creativity ring
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S. (1978). What makes giftedness? Reexamining a definition. Phi Delta Kappan, 60(3), 180-184.

tail_precision_rationale: A reasoning cutoff never observes how many and how varied the ideas a child can generate for an open class. M-IDEAFLU gives a continuous ideation axis, but at the gifted tail M-FLEX (how many distinct sub-kinds the child spans - for 'round things': food, toys, nature, body) and M-ORIG (statistical infrequency of instances vs a norm bank) are the sharp separators between a child who lists ten near-identical items and one who ranges widely and rarely. M-EXPLORE (breadth of the drifting field sampled plus self-generated additions) distinguishes systematic idea search from narrow fixation, a process signal the uses-based Brainstorm Blaster, the consequences-based What-If World, and the improvement-based Toy Tune-Up do not collect. M-ENGAGE gates the signal so idle time is never scored as low creativity.
age_rationale: Generating instances of a concrete property is developmentally accessible from kindergarten because the child only taps matching pictures (no reading) and can add ideas by stamp or draw, directly serving the K-1 Instances format; categories scale from perceptual (round, noisy) for the youngest to abstract or relational (things that come in pairs, things that can be recycled) for 6-8, who add ideas by typing, so the same generate-many-instances mechanic holds across all bands.

adaptive.content_range: concrete perceptual categories (round things, things that make noise) for young children up to abstract or relational categories (things that come in pairs, things that can be recycled) for older
adaptive.difficulty_levers: category abstractness, breadth vs narrowness of the class, richness of the picture field, time-window length
adaptive.notes: Not accuracy-adaptive: there is no single difficulty ladder, so adaptivity means selecting categories of varying abstractness and tuning the idea window; branching is on category type, not on right or wrong.

engagement_hook: A playful round-up where matching ideas leap into a basket with a satisfying pop and a combo meter rewards jumping to a brand-new kind of idea, turning 'name everything that...' into a fast, chase-the-next-idea game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Vocabulary and world knowledge can confound how many instances a child names (offer picture-tap and stamp/draw modes to lower the language load and interpret against local norms); a rich picture field can cue ideas and inflate fluency (rotate fields and score self-generated additions separately); automated originality scoring has low reliability and can misjudge child-appropriate ideas (use per-category norm banks and human/expert audit); impulsive rapid tapping can inflate raw counts (score distinct on-category ideas and sub-category flexibility, not tap speed).

name: Shape-Maker Studio
one_liner: Given a handful of plain shapes, the child arranges and combines them into as many different recognizable pictures as they can, making something new each time.
interaction: A palette of basic shapes (circles, triangles, squares, arcs) sits beside a canvas. The child drags shapes onto the canvas, arranges and rotates them into a recognizable thing, names it (picture-menu for pre-readers, text for older), then taps 'New idea' for a fresh canvas to build something different. The engine logs how many distinct pictures are completed, how rare each depicted thing is, how many shapes and added details each uses, how many different kinds of thing they span, and the build sequence. Nothing is graded right or wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand dragging a circle onto a triangle to make an ice-cream cone, tapping 'New,' then combining a square and triangle into a house, then arcs into a fish - three different pictures from the same shapes - cueing 'build it into something, then something new.' One unscored warm-up canvas lets the child combine two shapes before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Figural divergent thinking (constructing pictures from given elements) captures creative potential with minimal language load
learning_science.why: Verbal creativity tasks confound creativity with vocabulary, whereas figural construction lets non-verbal and multilingual children show originality
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an open figural-construction canvas scored for fluency, originality, and elaboration to broaden who can demonstrate creativity (H4)
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Norms-Technical Manual. Bensenville, IL: Scholastic Testing Service.

learning_science.principle: Creative generation is shaped by structured imagination - how a person recombines category-structured elements into novel exemplars
learning_science.why: Building recognizable things from abstract shapes exercises the generative recombination at the heart of creative cognition, distinct from selecting an answer
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide combinable shapes and score the variety and category-span of exemplars produced (M-FLEX, M-IDEAFLU) alongside originality
learning_science.source: Ward, T. B. (1994). Structured imagination: The role of category structure in exemplar generation. Cognitive Psychology, 27(1), 1-40.

learning_science.principle: Open creative products are validly evaluated by expert consensus, since automated originality scoring is unreliable
learning_science.why: Figural products have no answer key, so appropriately reliable scoring comes from trained judges rating novelty and quality
learning_science.concrete_decision: Persist each construction as a reviewable artifact so a Consensual Assessment panel can rate originality, not just the automated counts
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

tail_precision_rationale: CogAT figural items ask the child to pick a completion, never to construct one, so creative production is unobserved. Here M-IDEAFLU (distinct pictures built) and M-ORIG (how rare each depicted thing is vs a norm bank) provide a production-based creativity axis; M-ELAB (shapes and added detail per picture) and M-FLEX (how many different categories of thing - animal, vehicle, food, structure - the child spans) separate broad, elaborated creators from those who repeat one motif; and M-PATH (the construction sequence) reveals deliberate composition versus random placement. This construct-from-parts shell is distinct from the draw-over-a-line Squiggle Studio and the stamp-features-on-a-toy Toy Tune-Up, and at the gifted tail it exposes figural creative-productive potential a multiple-choice cutoff cannot see, especially for non-verbal and multilingual children. M-ENGAGE gates the signal so idle time is not read as low creativity.
age_rationale: Dragging and combining a few large shapes on a canvas is accessible from kindergarten and needs no reading (names come from a picture menu), directly serving the 2-3 Pattern/Line-Meanings gap while remaining valid younger and older; older children build more, more-original, and more-elaborated pictures and name them by typing, but the same construct-from-shapes mechanic holds across all bands.

adaptive.content_range: a few simple shapes for young builders up to richer palettes and constraints (make something that moves, use every shape) for older
adaptive.difficulty_levers: palette size and shape variety, presence of construction constraints, canvas affordances (rotate/resize), time-window length
adaptive.notes: Open production, not accuracy-adaptive: vary the shape palette and any construction constraints; branching selects stimulus or constraint richness rather than scoring correctness.

engagement_hook: A tactile art studio where plain shapes snap together into whatever the child imagines and each 'New idea' wipes the canvas clean for the next invention - watching a pile of shapes become a fish or a rocket is its own reward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fine-motor and device-drag skill can limit construction fidelity (score idea count, category-span, and intent, not neatness; use large snap targets and allow simple placement); touch vs mouse hardware differences add noise (normalize by device); automated originality of constructions is unreliable (retain artifacts for consensual expert rating and flag scoring reliability); a child who fixates on one motif may under-produce despite ability (interpret flexibility and originality alongside, not just fluency).

name: Story Studio
one_liner: The child composes an original short illustrated story across a few panels toward a loose prompt, then explains their choices in a brief 'tell me about your story' reflection.
interaction: Given a loose brief (tell a story about someone who finds something surprising), the child fills three panels by dragging in characters, settings, and props, arranging a beginning, middle, and end, and adding a caption per panel (picture/emoji menu for young children, short text for older). On finishing they tap through a short structured reflection ('What happens?', 'What was the problem?', 'How does it end?'). The engine logs build time and order, panels completed over time, elements and detail per panel, reworks, and stores the story plus reflection as an artifact for later rubric or consensual scoring.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand dropping a puppy into panel one, a park into panel two, and a reunion into panel three - a tiny beginning-middle-end taking shape while a star meter fills - then tapping the reflection thumbs, cueing 'make a story across the panels, then tell about it.' An unscored warm-up lets the child fill a single panel before the real brief.

learning_science.principle: Authentic, open-ended product creation with reflection (Renzulli Type III) demonstrates real creative-productive giftedness
learning_science.why: Self-directed composition and reflection reveal applied, real-world ability that timed multiple-choice items cannot elicit
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an open compose-and-reflect story task scored by rubric for reasoning, originality, and follow-through rather than a keyed item
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S., & Reis, S. M. (2014). The Schoolwide Enrichment Model: A How-to Guide for Talent Development (3rd ed.). Waco, TX: Prufrock Press.

learning_science.principle: Narrative is a distinct mode of thought for organizing experience into meaning
learning_science.why: Composing a coherent story with intention, problem, and resolution samples a meaning-making capacity that logical-scientific authentic tasks do not
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score narrative structure (setup, problem, resolution) and coherence as a polytomous product signal distinct from mechanical or scientific authentic tasks
learning_science.source: Bruner, J. (1986). Actual Minds, Possible Worlds. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.

learning_science.principle: Open creative products are validly and reliably evaluated by expert consensus (Consensual Assessment Technique)
learning_science.why: A composed story has no answer key, so defensible scoring comes from multiple trained raters judging originality and quality
learning_science.concrete_decision: Persist each story and reflection as an artifact and score with a multi-rater anchored rubric (M-RUBRIC) to obtain inter-rater reliability
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

tail_precision_rationale: Multiple-choice batteries cannot observe creative composition or narrative reasoning. M-RUBRIC (multi-rater rubric quality of the story) and M-POLY (graded narrative structure and reflection depth) turn one authentic product into a rich polytomous signal, while M-ELAB (elements and detail per panel) and M-REV (reworking panels rather than accepting a first pass) describe the craft behind it, and M-PROG (panels completed over time) turns the composition into a trajectory that shows whether a child builds a whole arc or stalls. This narrative-composition channel is deliberately distinct from the mechanical build-and-reflect Maker's Workshop and the science-investigation Investigation Station, and at the gifted tail it reveals creative-productive potential - the Renzulli Type III profile - for verbally and visually expressive children whom notation-heavy items miss. M-ENGAGE gates the signal so idle time is not read as low achievement.
age_rationale: Open panel composition suits many ages, but a meaningful story arc and a structured reflection (naming the problem and resolution) depend on narrative and metacognitive skills more reliable from about grade 2 upward; K-1 is served instead by the concrete creativity and exploration types, while 2-3 composes with a picture/emoji caption-and-reflection menu and 6-8 writes short text, directly serving the 4-5 authentic-performance gap.

adaptive.content_range: simple three-panel stories with picture captions (2-3) up to multi-panel stories with written captions and a constrained brief (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: brief openness or constraints, number of panels, richness of the element palette, depth of the required reflection
adaptive.notes: Open production, not accuracy-adaptive: vary brief constraints, panel count, and reflection depth by age; adaptivity is selecting brief complexity and follow-up reflection prompts, and optionally probing deeper when a story is rich.

engagement_hook: A comic-strip studio where kids drag characters and scenes into panels and watch their own story come to life, then get to show and tell it - creative ownership plus storytelling is intrinsically motivating.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Open composition has low scoring reliability (require multiple trained raters, anchored rubrics, and report inter-rater agreement); rubric halo and rater bias inflate or deflate scores (blind raters to child identity and use diverse panels); reflection and caption quality confound verbal ability with narrative merit (score product and reflection separately; use picture/emoji menus for young and EL children); fine-motor or device skill can limit composition (score narrative intent, not neatness); time available strongly shapes elaboration (standardize the compose window).

name: Fix-It Crew
one_liner: The child watches a short social or school situation and puts the possible responses in order from works-best to works-worst on a three-shelf ladder.
interaction: A voiced/animated scenario plays, then 3 pictured response options appear scrambled in a tray. The child taps an option then taps one of three shelves (Works best / Just okay / Works worst), can re-place any option to reorder freely, and taps 'Lock it in' when all three are placed. Each ordering is scored against an expert-consensus rank key by counting concordant option-pairs (partial credit) plus whether the single best option is on top; the engine logs placement order, re-orderings, deliberation time, and an optional confidence tap.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a scene, then the hand tapping the 'wider base' idea and placing it on the top 'works best' shelf while a weaker idea stays low - cueing 'best idea on top, worst on the bottom.' One unscored warm-up scenario (a wobbly block tower) lets the child order two ideas before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Situational judgment tests validly assess practical/social judgment from responses to realistic scenarios
learning_science.why: Applied judgment predicts adjustment and achievement but is untouched by abstract reasoning items
learning_science.concrete_decision: Key scenario items to an expert-consensus effectiveness scale so judgment is scored on a defensible standard rather than opinion
learning_science.source: McDaniel, M. A., Hartman, N. S., Whetzel, D. L., & Grubb, W. L. (2007). Situational judgment tests, response instructions, and validity: A meta-analysis. Personnel Psychology, 60(1), 63-91.

learning_science.principle: A rank-all-options (most-effective) SJT response format yields more information per item and resists response distortion better than pick-one
learning_science.why: Ordering every option exposes fine gradations of judgment and lowers the ceiling where many pick the obviously-nice answer
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ask the child to rank all options most-to-least effective and score concordant pairs (a polytomous signal) rather than a single best pick
learning_science.source: Weekley, J. A., & Ployhart, R. E. (Eds.). (2006). Situational Judgment Tests: Theory, Measurement, and Application. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

learning_science.principle: Task-approach judgment (handling hard, boring, or frustrating work) reflects conscientiousness and self-regulation
learning_science.why: Choosing persistence and help-seeking strategies in scenarios reveals dispositions that predict school success
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include a conscientiousness/effort scenario and credit orderings that rank adaptive self-regulatory responses highest
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. L., & Seligman, M. E. P. (2005). Self-discipline outdoes IQ in predicting academic performance of adolescents. Psychological Science, 16(12), 939-944.

tail_precision_rationale: The existing single-best-pick SJT scores only whether the top option was found; here the child must grade every option, so M-POLY (concordant option-pairs vs the expert rank key) extracts far more tail information from one rich item while M-ACC (best option on top) preserves the sharp top-end signal. M-PATH (order of placements) and M-REV (re-orderings before committing) separate deliberate, confident sorters from trial-and-error, M-RT indexes reflection, and M-CONF calibration down-weights lucky orderings. Ordering resolves near-ties that a pick-one item collapses, sharpening judgment placement exactly where equally 'able' children differ.
age_rationale: Ordering three options requires holding and comparing several responses at once, which is unreliable at K-1 (served instead by the single-pick animated SJT); from about grade 2 upward children can rank a few options, with voiced scenarios and pictured choices for 2-3 and richer text dilemmas with 4 options for 6-8.

adaptive.content_range: one-step social scenes with 3 options (young) up to multi-consideration dilemmas with 4 options and subtle best answers (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of options to rank, closeness of option effectiveness, subtlety of the best choice, competing goods within a scenario
adaptive.notes: Difficulty adapts by option count and how close options are in effectiveness; scoring is consensus-keyed concordant-pair credit rather than a pure ability theta.

engagement_hook: A 'fix-it crew' framing where the child ranks ways to solve a problem on a three-shelf podium - sorting ideas best-to-worst feels like judging a contest rather than taking a test.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Ranked choices are semi-self-report and partly fakeable/social-desirability-prone (mitigate with decision timing, forced trade-offs between two goods, and consequence-free framing); working-memory and reading load rise with option count (cap options, voice scenarios, use pictures); expert-consensus rank keys can encode cultural or rater bias (use diverse, bias-audited panels and localize keys); fine ranking of near-equal options may exceed young children's resolution (keep option effectiveness well separated for 2-3).

name: Better Move
one_liner: Across a run of quick two-option choices, the child taps the better response to each little social or school situation.
interaction: Each trial shows a one-line voiced situation and two pictured responses side by side; the child taps the better move and the next pair appears immediately. Some pairs are parallel repeats presented in swapped order to test consistency. The engine scores agreement with an expert-consensus key per pair (accuracy), a running net-effectiveness score, per-pair reaction time, choice consistency across the parallel pairs, and effort drift across the run.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a kid dropping a teddy and the hand tapping 'help pick it up' over 'ignore them' with a happy result - cueing 'tap the kinder, smarter move.' One unscored warm-up pair precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Situational judgment tests validly predict real-world behavior and show less adverse impact than cognitive tests
learning_science.why: Applied social/practical judgment adds incremental validity beyond ability and broadens equitable identification
learning_science.concrete_decision: Assess judgment with scenario items keyed to expert consensus rather than a self-rated trait scale
learning_science.source: McDaniel, M. A., Hartman, N. S., Whetzel, D. L., & Grubb, W. L. (2007). Situational judgment tests, response instructions, and validity: A meta-analysis. Personnel Psychology, 60(1), 63-91.

learning_science.principle: Forced-choice / paired-comparison formats reduce halo, acquiescence, and social-desirability distortion relative to single-stimulus ratings
learning_science.why: Repeated binary comparisons make faking harder and yield many quick, reliable data points
learning_science.concrete_decision: Deliver judgment as many rapid two-option comparisons and insert parallel repeated pairs to estimate internal consistency
learning_science.source: Brown, A., & Maydeu-Olivares, A. (2011). Item response modeling of forced-choice questionnaires. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 71(3), 460-502.

learning_science.principle: Animated, low-reading situational judgment can assess young children's social decision-making in a game
learning_science.why: Interactive scenarios reduce reading load and raise ecological validity for social-emotional skills
learning_science.concrete_decision: Voice each situation and use pictured options so pre/early readers can compare responses
learning_science.source: DeRosier, M. E., & Thomas, J. M. (2019). Establishing the criterion validity of Zoo U's game-based social-emotional skills assessment. Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment, 37(3), 341-354.

tail_precision_rationale: Many fast binary judgments accumulate into a reliable score (M-ACC agreement per pair; M-POLY net effectiveness) with less halo than rating scales, so small true differences in judgment separate cleanly at the tail. M-CONSIST (same choice on swapped parallel pairs) flags children whose responses are stable versus noisy - a reliability gate that tightens conditional confidence near the cut - and M-DRIFT catches fading effort so late low-effort choices do not bias the estimate. This paired-comparison shell is deliberately distinct from single-best-pick and rank-all SJTs and contributes a coach-resistant, high-trial judgment axis.
age_rationale: Comparing two pictured responses is a simple binary choice suitable from about grade 2 with voicing; the youngest band is served by the single-pick animated SJT. Older children get subtler pairs and more trials while the two-option mechanic is unchanged.

adaptive.content_range: obvious kind-vs-unkind pairs (young) up to near-tie pairs distinguishing good from slightly-better responses (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: closeness of the two options in effectiveness, scenario subtlety, number of pairs, time pressure
adaptive.notes: Naturally adaptive: route stronger judges into closer near-tie pairs to find their judgment frontier; parallel pairs are inserted for the consistency estimate, not to fit a pure theta.

engagement_hook: A snappy 'which is the better move?' game of quick taps with instant feedback - the fast rhythm and simple two-way choice keep it light and playable for the youngest testable band.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Binary judgments remain semi-self-report and partly fakeable (use reaction-time flooring to catch reflexive tapping, forced trade-offs, and consequence-free framing); very fast pacing can reward impulsivity (interpret with M-RT and discard implausibly fast responses); consensus keys can encode cultural/rater bias (diverse bias-audited panels, locale checks); low consistency can reflect fatigue rather than poor judgment (gate with M-DRIFT/M-ENGAGE).

name: Sort-It-Out
one_liner: The child tidies a pile of mixed things into the right bins, and how carefully and completely they do it is the measure.
interaction: A tray of mixed pictured items (fruit, toys, clothes) sits above three labeled bins. The child taps an item then taps a bin to file it; a misfiled item is flagged and can be tapped to pull back and re-file. An always-visible 'I'm all done' button lets the child stop at any time. The engine logs each placement's correctness, careless misfiles versus systematic errors, self-corrections, whether sorting proceeds kind-by-kind or scattered, how much of the pile is completed before stopping, and whether carefulness fades across the pile.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the hand picking an apple and dropping it into the fruit bin with a satisfying click, leaving a toy for the toy bin - cueing 'put each thing where it belongs.' One unscored warm-up with three items precedes the full pile.

learning_science.principle: Conscientiousness (orderliness, carefulness, follow-through) predicts achievement over and above cognitive ability
learning_science.why: A work-habits signal broadens a gifted battery beyond reasoning and is absent from CogAT
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score careful, complete, orderly sorting behaviorally rather than administering fakeable conscientiousness self-report
learning_science.source: Roberts, B. W., Lejuez, C., Krueger, R. F., Richards, J. M., & Hill, P. L. (2014). What is conscientiousness and how can it be assessed? Developmental Psychology, 50(5), 1315-1330.

learning_science.principle: Effortful control - the self-regulatory temperament root of conscientiousness - is observable in early childhood and predicts later outcomes
learning_science.why: Young children cannot reliably self-report traits, but careful, sustained, rule-consistent behavior can be observed directly
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an observable sort-and-tidy task (sustained accuracy, self-correction, completion) as an early behavioral index for pre-readers
learning_science.source: Rothbart, M. K., Ahadi, S. A., Hershey, K. L., & Fisher, P. (2001). Investigations of temperament at three to seven years: The Children's Behavior Questionnaire. Child Development, 72(5), 1394-1408.

learning_science.principle: Whether a child monitors and repairs errors is an informative behavioral signal, not just noise
learning_science.why: Catching and fixing one's own mistakes indexes conscientious self-monitoring distinct from ability
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log misfile types and self-corrections (checking behavior) as carefulness indicators rather than treating all errors as random
learning_science.source: Eisenberg, N., Duckworth, A. L., Spinrad, T. L., & Valiente, C. (2014). Conscientiousness: Origins in childhood? Developmental Psychology, 50(5), 1331-1349.

tail_precision_rationale: Reasoning tests never observe how carefully or completely a child works. M-ERRTYPE (careless misfiles vs systematic mistakes) and M-REV (catching and fixing one's own errors) index carefulness and self-monitoring; M-PATH (systematic kind-by-kind sorting vs scattered) indexes orderliness; M-PERSIST (finishing the whole pile vs stopping early) indexes follow-through; and M-DRIFT (whether error rate rises late) indexes self-regulation stamina. Together these behavioral conscientiousness facets add a non-cognitive tail axis - flagging high-ability, low-diligence profiles a reasoning-only cut over-selects - and, crucially, they reach the K-1 band where self-report and the diligence-vs-distraction task are not usable.
age_rationale: Sorting familiar objects into a few labeled bins is developmentally appropriate from kindergarten and needs only tapping and no reading (bins are pictured), directly serving the K-1 early-conscientiousness/effortful-control item; by upper elementary careful sorting ceilings, so the type targets the youngest bands where the diligence-vs-distraction and self-report conscientiousness types do not apply.

adaptive.content_range: a small pile with 2-3 obvious categories (K-1) up to a larger pile with more categories and closer look-alikes (2-3)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: pile size, number of categories, similarity of items across bins, presence of ambiguous items, time available
adaptive.notes: Not accuracy-adaptive in the IRT sense: the signal is carefulness and completion. Adaptivity means tuning pile size and category count to age and optionally lengthening the pile to see whether carefulness is sustained.

engagement_hook: A satisfying tidy-up game where each item clicks into its bin - the simple, orderly pleasure of sorting is itself the draw for young children.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Early self-regulation is developmentally noisy, so single-session tail separation is modest (interpret with other non-cognitive types and repeat measures); fine-motor slips can masquerade as careless misfiles (use large targets and log error type); a child bored by tidying may stop early despite high ability, not low follow-through (gate with M-ENGAGE and never frame stopping as failure); category knowledge is a mild confound (use universally familiar objects and a warm-up).

name: Wonder Room
one_liner: Given a plain box and a strange, sparkly box, the child repeatedly chooses which to open, then freely explores a room of mystery objects - revealing what draws their curiosity.
interaction: On each trial two covered boxes appear - one plain, one visibly novel/complex (sparkling, animated) - and the child taps whichever they want to open to reveal a small surprise. After several such choices, a free-exploration room of covered objects (some plain, some strange) invites the child to open whatever they like, with an always-visible 'I'm done'. The engine logs the share of novel-over-plain choices, how quickly the child reaches for the novel option, how many distinct objects they open when free, and whether they seek the strangest ones first.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the hand passing the plain box and tapping the sparkly one, which pops open to a unicorn - cueing 'open whatever makes you wonder.' One unscored warm-up choice (either box gives a fun reveal) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Curiosity is driven by collative properties of stimuli - novelty, complexity, and surprise - that motivate exploration
learning_science.why: A behavioral pull toward the novel and complex is a direct index of curiosity that reasoning tests never elicit
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer repeated novel-vs-familiar choices and score the preference for novelty/complexity (M-UNCERT) rather than asking whether the child is curious
learning_science.source: Berlyne, D. E. (1960). Conflict, Arousal, and Curiosity. New York: McGraw-Hill.

learning_science.principle: Children's scientific curiosity can be operationalized behaviorally as preference for and exploration of uncertainty/novelty
learning_science.why: Behavioral exploration avoids the social-desirability ceilings of curiosity questionnaires and works for pre-readers
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score novelty-choice proportion and breadth/order of free exploration from action logs instead of self-report
learning_science.source: Jirout, J., & Klahr, D. (2012). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review, 32(2), 125-160.

learning_science.principle: Interest/curiosity is a distinct motivational engine of learning and knowledge-building
learning_science.why: An intrinsic pull toward the unknown sustains the self-directed learning behind gifted development
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include a no-reward free-exploration window so the choice to explore reflects intrinsic interest, not incentives
learning_science.source: Hidi, S., & Renninger, K. A. (2006). The four-phase model of interest development. Educational Psychologist, 41(2), 111-127.

tail_precision_rationale: A reasoning cutoff observes performance under instruction, never what a child gravitates toward when free. M-UNCERT (proportion of novel/complex over plain/known choices) is a direct behavioral curiosity axis, and M-RTFIRST (how quickly the child reaches for the novel option) adds an approach-motivation signal. In the free room, M-EXPLORE (distinct objects opened) and M-PATH (whether the strangest are sought first) distinguish broad, self-directed explorers from narrow ones. At the tail this separates an able-but-incurious child from an able-and-curious one - the curiosity ring central to sustained gifted achievement - and, unlike the Mystery Box, it isolates novelty preference itself (no reward gamble) and needs no question-asking, reaching the pre-verbal K-1 band.
age_rationale: Choosing which box to open and freely opening objects need only tapping and no language, so K-1 can fully participate, directly serving the K-1 curiosity item; the mechanic is deliberately pre-verbal (no question composition), so it complements the question-based Question Quest that starts at 2-3, and novelty-preference variance is richest and most interpretable in the youngest bands.

adaptive.content_range: a few plain-vs-novel choices and a small room (K-1) up to more choices, finer novelty gradations, and a larger room (2-3)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: degree of novelty/complexity contrast between options, number of choices, room size, resolvable vs open-ended surprises
adaptive.notes: Not accuracy-adaptive: the signal is preference and exploration breadth. Adaptivity means grading the novelty contrast and room size, and optionally extending free time when engagement stays high to gauge how deep exploratory drive runs.

engagement_hook: Sparkly mystery boxes and a room full of things to pop open - the irresistible pull to see what's inside is exactly the curiosity being measured.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Novelty-seeking can reflect sensation-seeking or impulsivity rather than epistemic curiosity (triangulate with the Mystery Box and Question Quest, and score exploration order/breadth, not raw clicking); single-session estimates are noisy (repeat across activities); prior exposure to similar toys is a familiarity confound (use novel objects and a warm-up); surprises must never be scary or punishing so avoidance is not mistaken for low curiosity; gate all signals with M-ENGAGE.

name: Show-and-Tell Studio
topics_techniques_covered: tell me about what you made interview
one_liner: A young child makes a quick creation on a sticker-and-color canvas, then tells about it through a spoken, picture-guided 'what did you make?' reflection.
interaction: The child taps picture-stamps (animals, houses, sun, rocket) and colors onto an open canvas, placing and removing elements freely to make anything they like. Tapping 'Done - tell about it' opens a pre-reader reflection: picture-answer prompts ('What is it?', 'What does it do?', 'Favorite part?') plus a hold-to-talk voice note. The engine stores the drawing and reflection as an artifact for later expert/consensual rating and logs elements placed, distinct kinds and colors used, detail added, reflection prompts answered, voice-note length, and time invested.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the hand tapping a house onto the canvas, then a sun, then tapping the reflection thumbs - cueing 'make something, then tell about it.' The warm-up lets the child place one sticker before the real creation.

learning_science.principle: A structured 'tell me about what you made' account of a self-chosen creation reveals demonstrated achievement and creative thinking in young children
learning_science.why: Oral reflection on a real product surfaces elaboration, originality, and persistence that pre-readers cannot show on multiple-choice items
learning_science.concrete_decision: Pair an open creation with a voiced, picture-guided reflection and score product-and-reflection quality rather than a keyed item
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S., & Reis, S. M. (2014). The Schoolwide Enrichment Model: A How-to Guide for Talent Development (3rd ed.). Waco, TX: Prufrock Press.

learning_science.principle: Open creative products are validly evaluated by expert consensus (Consensual Assessment Technique)
learning_science.why: A self-chosen creation has no answer key, so reliable scoring comes from multiple trained judges rating novelty and quality
learning_science.concrete_decision: Persist each drawing and reflection as a reviewable artifact scored by a multi-rater rubric (M-RUBRIC) with reported agreement
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

learning_science.principle: Performance/authentic assessment broadens who can demonstrate ability (H4) by lowering the reading/notation barrier
learning_science.why: Hands-on making with oral reflection lets pre- and early readers show higher-order capability
learning_science.concrete_decision: Deliver the task as tap-to-place stickers with a voiced picture-menu reflection so non-readers fully participate
learning_science.source: Wiggins, G. (1993). Assessing Student Performance: Exploring the Purpose and Limits of Testing. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

tail_precision_rationale: Multiple-choice items cannot observe creative production, and the 2-3-and-up build-and-reflect types exclude pre-readers. Here M-RUBRIC (multi-rater rating of the stored creation and its reflection) and M-POLY (graded reflection depth across the picture prompts and voice note) turn one authentic product into a rich polytomous signal, while M-ELAB (elements, distinct kinds, colors, added detail) and M-PERSIST (time invested and late additions) describe the process. At the tail this reveals creative-productive potential - Renzulli's Type III profile - for K-1 children who cannot yet show it on notation-heavy items, closing the demonstrated-achievement gap at the youngest band.
age_rationale: Tapping stickers and answering voiced picture prompts (plus an optional hold-to-talk note) need no reading or writing, so K-1 can fully participate - directly serving the K-1 'tell me about what you made' item; the 2-3-and-up build-and-reflect, investigation, and story types cover older bands, so this type is scoped to the pre-reader bands it uniquely serves.

adaptive.content_range: a small sticker palette with three picture-prompt reflections (K-1) up to a richer palette and slightly deeper prompts (2-3)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: palette richness, openness vs a loose theme, number/depth of reflection prompts, availability of a voice note
adaptive.notes: Open production, not accuracy-adaptive: vary palette and reflection depth by age; adaptivity is selecting theme openness and follow-up prompts, optionally probing further when a creation is rich.

engagement_hook: A playful sticker studio plus a friendly 'show and tell' - young children love making something of their own and then getting to say what it is.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Open products score with low reliability (require multiple trained, identity-blind raters, anchored rubrics, and reported inter-rater agreement); oral reflection confounds language ability with creative merit (score product and reflection separately; picture menus for EL/young); home enrichment and device/motor skill differ (score intent, not neatness); standardize the make-and-tell window; voice capture raises privacy duties (store artifacts under strict consent and access controls).

name: Master Builder
one_liner: The child builds a structure by stacking chosen blocks across a row of columns toward the loose goal of something tall and interesting, then the creation is saved for rating.
interaction: A palette of colored blocks and decoration pieces (door, window, flag) sits above a five-column build site. The child picks a block and taps a column to stack it, taps 'Undo' to remove and rework, and taps 'I'm finished' when satisfied. The engine samples the build's growth over time and logs total blocks, height, distinct block kinds, decorations, and re-workings; the finished structure is stored as an artifact for later expert/consensual rating on ingenuity, originality, and elaboration.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the hand stacking three blocks into a column and topping it with a flag - cueing 'stack blocks to build something.' One unscored warm-up lets the child place a block or two before the real build.

learning_science.principle: Authentic, open-ended product creation demonstrates real creative-productive giftedness (Renzulli Type III)
learning_science.why: Self-directed construction reveals applied ingenuity and follow-through that timed multiple-choice items cannot elicit
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an open build task rated by rubric for ingenuity, originality, and elaboration rather than a keyed item
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S., & Reis, S. M. (2014). The Schoolwide Enrichment Model: A How-to Guide for Talent Development (3rd ed.). Waco, TX: Prufrock Press.

learning_science.principle: Constructive play and block building reveal early spatial-creative competence and planning
learning_science.why: Structured block construction is a developmentally rich window into young children's design thinking and elaboration
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the structure's complexity, variety, and iterative refinement as evidence of demonstrated achievement
learning_science.source: Casey, B. M., Andrews, N., Schindler, H., Kersh, J. E., Samper, A., & Copley, J. (2008). The development of spatial skills through interventions involving block building activities. Cognition and Instruction, 26(3), 269-309.

learning_science.principle: Open creative products are validly evaluated by expert consensus (Consensual Assessment Technique)
learning_science.why: A free-form build has no answer key, so reliable scoring comes from multiple trained judges
learning_science.concrete_decision: Persist each structure as a reviewable artifact scored by a multi-rater rubric (M-RUBRIC) with reported agreement
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

tail_precision_rationale: Reasoning items score whether a child knows an answer, never what a child can make. M-RUBRIC (multi-rater rating of the stored structure) anchors the tail signal in authentic ingenuity, while M-PROG (how the build grows - a steady, planful arc versus an early stall) and M-REV (undo/rework to improve) expose the construction process, and M-ELAB (blocks, kinds, decorations, height) grades product complexity. This engineering-construction shell is distinct from the snap-a-machine Maker's Workshop and the science Investigation Station, and it reaches the K-1 band those types exclude, closing the demonstrated-achievement gap for hands-on young builders whom notation-heavy items miss.
age_rationale: Stacking blocks by tapping needs no reading and is developmentally accessible from kindergarten, directly serving the K-1 demonstrated-achievement band; older children build taller, more varied, and more elaborated structures, but the tap-to-stack mechanic and rubric scoring hold across bands, so the type spans K-1 through 4-5 while the reflection-heavy achievement types cover 2-3 and up.

adaptive.content_range: a few blocks and columns with a simple 'build something' invitation (young) up to richer palettes, more columns, and loose constraints ('build a home', 'make it tall and strong') for older
adaptive.difficulty_levers: palette size and variety, number of columns/space, presence of a loose goal or constraint, decoration options, build-window length
adaptive.notes: Open production, not accuracy-adaptive: vary palette, space, and constraints; adaptivity is selecting brief openness and probing deeper when a build is rich.

engagement_hook: A blocks playground where every tap stacks another piece and the tower visibly rises - building something of your own and crowning it with a flag is its own reward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Open products score with low reliability (require multiple trained, identity-blind raters, anchored rubrics, and reported agreement); fine-motor and device skill can limit build fidelity (score design intent, not neatness; large targets); block-play exposure at home is a familiarity confound (use a self-teaching warm-up); a simplified stacking model is not real physics, so rate design intent rather than structural correctness; standardize the build window.

name: Tune Maker
one_liner: The child composes a short tune by tapping colored notes onto a music grid and pressing play, shaping it however they like.
interaction: A grid of five colored pitch rows by eight time steps lets the child tap cells to place notes (each plays its tone), press play to hear the sequence sweep across the steps, remove notes, or clear and start over. The engine plays the composition and logs notes placed, distinct pitches used, steps filled, melodic contour, notes removed/reworked, plays, edits made after the first play, and time; the finished note pattern is stored as an artifact for later expert/consensual rating on originality and musical structure.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the hand tapping four cells that light up and sound, then pressing play so the notes sweep left to right - cueing 'tap squares to make music, then play it.' One unscored warm-up lets the child tap a few notes and play before composing for real.

learning_science.principle: Giftedness is domain-specific and includes musical/artistic talent beyond academic reasoning
learning_science.why: A defensible identification must let talent show in non-academic domains that CogAT does not sample
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide an auditory composition task so musically talented children can demonstrate achievement (H4)
learning_science.source: Gardner, H. (1983). Frames of Mind: The Theory of Multiple Intelligences. New York: Basic Books.

learning_science.principle: Authentic, open-ended creative production demonstrates creative-productive giftedness (Renzulli Type III)
learning_science.why: Composing an original tune reveals generative, iterative creative work that keyed items cannot elicit
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score an open composition by rubric for originality and structure, retaining the artifact, rather than a keyed item
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S., & Reis, S. M. (2014). The Schoolwide Enrichment Model: A How-to Guide for Talent Development (3rd ed.). Waco, TX: Prufrock Press.

learning_science.principle: Open creative products are validly evaluated by expert consensus (Consensual Assessment Technique)
learning_science.why: A composed tune has no answer key, so reliable scoring comes from multiple trained judges rating novelty and quality
learning_science.concrete_decision: Persist each composition as a reviewable artifact scored by a multi-rater rubric (M-RUBRIC) with reported agreement
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

tail_precision_rationale: Reasoning batteries cannot observe musical creation, and the other achievement types are visual, verbal, or scientific. M-RUBRIC (multi-rater rating of the stored tune) anchors the signal in authentic musical originality and structure; M-ELAB (notes, distinct pitches, steps, melodic contour) grades compositional richness; M-REV (removing/reworking notes) and M-PERSIST (editing after hearing a first play, time composing) reveal iterative craft. Adding an auditory production domain broadens who can reach the tail (H4) and closes the K-1 demonstrated-achievement gap with a mechanic wholly distinct from drawing, building, and storytelling.
age_rationale: Tapping cells on a grid and pressing play need no reading or musical notation and are accessible from kindergarten, serving the K-1 band; a pentatonic scale keeps every combination pleasant so young children are not penalized. Older children compose longer, more structured tunes, but the tap-a-grid mechanic holds across bands.

adaptive.content_range: a small grid on a pentatonic scale (young) up to more pitches, more steps, and optional tempo/pattern constraints (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size (pitches x steps), scale, tempo, presence of a target mood or pattern constraint, composition-window length
adaptive.notes: Open production, not accuracy-adaptive: vary grid size and constraints; adaptivity is selecting scale/length and probing deeper when a composition is rich.

engagement_hook: A colorful music grid where every tap makes a sound and pressing play turns the child's taps into a real little song - composing music is playful and instantly rewarding.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Open products score with low reliability (require multiple trained, identity-blind raters, anchored rubrics, and reported agreement); prior music training is a confound (use a self-teaching warm-up and interpret cautiously); the pentatonic scale makes any pattern sound consonant, so rate structure/originality rather than mere pleasantness; device audio quality varies (ensure a visual fallback); a child unmotivated by music will under-produce despite ability (offer the other achievement domains and gate with M-ENGAGE).
